subject: Science (GCSE Biology, Chemistry, Physics)
board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0
source: Lessons 1 to 20: first written from the school Science curriculum journey 2026-27 (Organic chemistry; Astrophysics) and Pearson Edexcel GCSE schemes, re-mapped to 4BI1 Biology 4, 4CH1 Chemistry 4 and 4PH1 Physics 8 (early-atmosphere lesson 9 retired as not on the International GCSE); orbital speed, red-shift and the HR diagram are 4PH1 content (red-shift, absolute magnitude and the HR diagram are Physics only, not Double Award) | Edexcel IGCSE 4BI1/4CH1 specification summary (content/syllabus/ks4/gcse-science.json), Y11 units Biology 3, Biology 4, Biology 5, Chemistry 3, Chemistry 4. Drive material not used. Not re-taught because covered by the existing lessons in content/lessons/gcse-science/y11.json: population, community, habitat, ecosystem and quadrats; biotic and abiotic factors; food chains, webs and pyramids and 10% energy transfer; carbon cycle; nitrogen cycle with named bacteria; pollution (sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, greenhouse gases, sewage and eutrophication) and deforestation (Biology 4 points 1, 3-7); hydrocarbons, formulae and homologous series, crude oil and fractional distillation, complete and incomplete combustion and acid rain, catalytic cracking, alkane and alkene reactions with the bromine water test, addition polymers (Chemistry 4 points 1 partly, 2-6, 8). Biology 4 biodiversity and distribution (point 2) and Chemistry 4 naming and isomers (point 1) are taught here. | Edexcel IGCSE Physics 4PH1 specification (units Physics 5-8, Y11). Existing UK-GCSE lessons in content/lessons/gcse-science/y11.json already cover Physics 8 gravity and the Solar System, g on other bodies, orbital speed (v = 2 pi r / T), life cycles of stars, colour and temperature, absolute magnitude and the HR diagram, red-shift and the CMB, so Physics 8 here adds orbits of comets and satellites and one consolidation lesson in exam terms. | Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Biology 4BI1 / Double Award 4SD0 specification | Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1 (and Science Double Award 4SD0) specification | Spring 1 2027 revision cycle 1 (lessons 86 to 105, weeks of 11 Jan to 1 Feb): Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Science (Double Award) 4SD0 Biology 1 to 2, Chemistry 1 to 2, Physics 1 to 4, with exam-style questions and mark schemes written for these lessons; the mock week (8 Feb) uses the school's mock papers | Spring 2 2027 revision cycle 2 (lessons 106 to 131, weeks of 15 Mar to 19 Apr, 5, 4, 3, 4, 5, 5 lessons): 4SD0 Biology 3 to 5, Chemistry 3 to 4, Physics 5 to 8 (Double Award points only), mock feedback, timed sections and repair lists towards the papers of 11, 18 and 25 May 2027, with exam-style questions and mark schemes written for these lessons; human reproduction (Biology 3.8 to 3.13) set as textbook independent study until the school confirms delivery

Extend: Explain why the placenta has a large surface area. [2 marks]
Stretch: Explain why a pregnant woman should avoid alcohol and smoking. [3 marks]
exit: State the roles of oestrogen and progesterone. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: describe how the fetus is nourished.
lessons.homework: Complete a summary sheet of the male and female systems and the cycle.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: labelled diagrams with a glossary; offer a teacher-led alternative if families request it. Stretch: describe how oestrogen and progesterone levels change across the menstrual cycle.

lessons.title: DNA, genes, the genome and protein synthesis
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a four-letter code build every protein in your body?
objectives: Describe the structure of DNA and the terms genome, gene, chromosome
Describe RNA and complementary base pairing
Describe transcription and translation in protein synthesis
successCriteria: All: describe the double helix and base pairing
Most: use base pairing to write complementary strands
Some: explain transcription and translation and how mutations affect proteins
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: bonding and polymers; Computing: coding
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the order in the code of life

keywords.def: all the genetic material of an organism
section of DNA that codes for a protein
three bases that code for one amino acid
messenger RNA copied from DNA that carries the code to the ribosome

starter: Bismillah. Where is DNA found in a human cell?

teach.heading: DNA and chromosomes
bullets: DNA is a double helix of two strands
Bases pair: A with T, C with G
The genome is all of an organism's DNA
teach.note: Each nucleotide has a phosphate, sugar and base. The human genome has about 3 billion base pairs and about 20 000 protein-coding genes. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes in the nucleus. Chromosomes are long coiled DNA with many genes.

model.problem: One DNA strand reads ATG CCA GTT. Write the complementary strand. If 20% of bases in a DNA sample are adenine, what are the percentages of the others?
steps: A pairs with T, C pairs with G
ATG CCA GTT pairs with TAC GGT CAA
model.answer: TAC GGT CAA; T 20%, C 30%, G 30%

teach.heading: RNA
bullets: Sugar is ribose; uracil (U) replaces thymine
teach.note: Compare with DNA: DNA double-stranded in the nucleus; RNA single-stranded and can leave the nucleus. U pairs with A.

teach.heading: Making a protein
bullets: Transcription: mRNA copies a gene in the nucleus
Translation: amino acids joined in the order coded by codons
teach.note: Transfer RNA brings amino acids. Each codon codes for one amino acid, e.g. UUU for phenylalanine. The order of amino acids decides the folding and shape, and shape decides function (enzyme active site).
cycle: Amino acids join to make a protein

teach.heading: A mistake in the code
bullets: A mutation changes the DNA base sequence
Protein shape and function may change
teach.note: Link to enzymes and cystic fibrosis: a change in one gene may lead to an enzyme or transport protein that does not fold correctly. Not every mutation changes the protein (the code has some redundancy).

misconception.wrong: Each gene makes a whole cell.
misconception.right: A gene codes for one protein. The cell's features come from many proteins working together.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils say T pairs with A in RNA; in RNA uracil pairs with A.

check.q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
check.why: RNA has uracil (U) instead of thymine (T).

practice: Write the complementary DNA strand to CGA TTC.
State where translation takes place.
Define gene and genome.
independent: Core: Draw a flow chart of protein synthesis.
Extend: The mRNA sequence is AUG CCA GUU. Write the DNA template strand that formed it. [2 marks]
Stretch: Explain how a mutation in a gene could cause an enzyme to stop working. [4 marks]
exit: State two differences between DNA and RNA. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: describe how the code becomes a protein.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph on how a gene becomes a protein, using at least six key terms.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: base-pair cards to physically match. Stretch: explain why the genetic code is described as universal.

lessons.title: Alleles and monohybrid crosses
lessons.bigQuestion: If both parents are tall, can a child be short?
objectives: Use the terms allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype and phenotype
Complete Punnett squares for monohybrid crosses
Describe codominance (Biology only)
successCriteria: All: define the key terms
Most: complete crosses and give ratios and probabilities
Some: explain codominance and work out parent genotypes from offspring
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: probability and ratio
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness and respect for the diversity in people

keywords.def: a different version of a gene
combination of alleles an organism has
the observable characteristic
both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote

starter: State the number of chromosomes in a human gamete.

teach.heading: Genetic vocabulary
bullets: Dominant allele shows in the heterozygote
Recessive allele shows only if there are two copies
Homozygous: two identical alleles; heterozygous: two different
teach.note: Use capital letter for dominant (T) and lower case for recessive (t). Genotype is the letters, phenotype is the visible trait. A pea plant Tt is tall; tt is dwarf.

teach.heading: Model: monohybrid cross
teach.note: Tt × Tt: gametes T, t from each parent. Offspring: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Phenotypes 3 tall : 1 dwarf. Probability of dwarf = 1 in 4 (25%). Also show Tt × tt giving 1 : 1.

model.problem: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt) are crossed. Give the genotype ratio, phenotype ratio and probability of a dwarf plant.
steps: Gametes: T or t from each parent
Square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt

teach.heading: Codominance (Biology only)
bullets: ABO blood group: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant
teach.note: Use letters I with superscripts A, B and O. Genotype IAIB gives group AB. Example: IAIO × IBIO gives A, B, AB or O in equal 1 in 4 chances.

misconception.wrong: The dominant allele is always the more common allele in a population.
misconception.right: Dominant means it shows in the heterozygote. It need not be the most common.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils say 100% because both parents are dominant phenotype; heterozygous parents can have recessive offspring.

check.q: Two heterozygous parents (Bb) have a child. What is the probability the child is bb?
check.why: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb, so one in four is bb.

practice: Define homozygous and heterozygous.
Give the phenotype of Tt where T is tall and dominant.
Complete a cross between Tt and tt.
independent: Core: Complete a Punnett square for Bb × Bb where B = brown eyes and b = blue eyes.
Extend: Parents with blood groups IAIO and IBIO: list the possible groups of their children. [3 marks]
Stretch: A tall plant crossed with a dwarf produces 48 tall and 52 dwarf offspring. Deduce the parent genotypes. [3 marks]
exit: Explain why two tall parents can have a short child. [3 marks]
Return to the big question using genotype language.
lessons.homework: Complete three crosses with Punnett squares and ratios.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: gamete cards to physically build squares. Stretch: what is a test cross?

lessons.title: Pedigrees, inherited disorders and sex determination
lessons.bigQuestion: Can we predict who will inherit a family condition?
objectives: Interpret family pedigrees and deduce genotypes
Explain inheritance of cystic fibrosis and Huntington's disease
Explain sex determination with XX and XY
successCriteria: All: describe sex determination
Most: interpret a simple pedigree
Some: calculate probabilities for carriers and future children
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: probability
lessons.smsc: Moral: compassion and respect for people with genetic conditions

keywords.def: a person who has one copy of a recessive allele but does not show the condition
family tree showing inheritance of a trait
X and Y chromosomes that determine sex
recessive disorder causing thick mucus in the lungs

starter: Bismillah. Cross Aa × Aa and give the ratio.
How many chromosomes in a human body cell?

teach.heading: Sex determination
bullets: Sperm carries X or Y: the sperm decides the sex
teach.note: A Punnett square gives 50% female and 50% male on average. Each pregnancy is independent, so a family with three girls has a 50% chance of a boy next. Probability of three girls in a row is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

teach.heading: Reading a pedigree
bullets: Squares male, circles female; shaded affected
Two unaffected parents with an affected child: recessive
Affected parents with unaffected child: dominant
teach.note: Describe: Parents are unaffected; of their four children, one daughter and one son have cystic fibrosis. Each unaffected parent must carry one recessive allele (Cc). A third unaffected child has a 2 in 3 chance of being a carrier.

model.problem: Both parents are unaffected. Their first child has cystic fibrosis (cc). Explain the parents' genotypes and the probability that their next child is affected.
steps: The child has cc: one c from each parent
Parents are unaffected so they must be Cc (carriers)
Cc × Cc gives CC, Cc, Cc, cc

teach.heading: Two inherited disorders
bullets: Cystic fibrosis: recessive, thick mucus in lungs and gut
Huntington's disease: dominant, nerve damage later in life
Only one H allele is needed to be affected
teach.note: For Huntington's, Hh × hh gives 50% chance of an affected child. Mention genetic counselling kindly; do not make pupils feel their own families are being analysed. Link to protein shape from the previous lesson.

misconception.wrong: A carrier of cystic fibrosis has the disease.
misconception.right: A carrier has one recessive allele and does not have the disease. Two copies are needed.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils think a family with three girls is 'due' a boy.

check.q: A couple already have three daughters. What is the probability that their fourth child is a boy?
check.why: Each birth is independent, so the probability is 1 in 2.

practice: State which parent decides the sex of a child.
Explain what is meant by a carrier.
Give the genotype of someone with Huntington's disease who has one affected parent.
independent: Core: Draw a Punnett square for XX × XY and give the ratio.
Extend: A man with Huntington's disease (Hh) and an unaffected woman (hh) have a child. Give the probability of the child being affected. [2 marks]
Stretch: Draw a pedigree for a family where two unaffected parents have two affected children and one unaffected child; label genotypes. [4 marks]
exit: Define phenotype and genotype. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: what can a pedigree predict and what can it not?
lessons.homework: Design and solve two pedigree problems for a partner.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded pedigree symbols. Stretch: sex-linked inheritance of red–green colour blindness.

lessons.title: Mitosis, meiosis and chromosome numbers
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do you keep 46 chromosomes in every body cell but make gametes with only 23?
objectives: Describe mitosis and its roles
Describe meiosis and why it produces genetically different haploid gametes
Use chromosome numbers in diploid and haploid cells
successCriteria: All: state the outcomes of mitosis and meiosis
Most: compare the two processes and give chromosome numbers
Some: explain how meiosis and fertilisation create variation
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: powers of two
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on the order in cell division and life's continuity

keywords.def: cell with two sets of chromosomes (46 in humans)
cell with one set of chromosomes (23 in humans)
cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid cells
cell division that produces four genetically different haploid gametes

starter: Bismillah. What does a gamete contain?
State where DNA is stored in a human cell.

teach.heading: Mitosis
bullets: One division produces two identical daughter cells
Same chromosome number as the parent cell
Used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction
teach.note: DNA is copied first so each daughter cell gets a full set. Uncontrolled mitosis forms tumours (cancer).

teach.heading: Meiosis and variation
teach.note: Reasons for difference: chromosomes shuffle into gametes randomly. With 23 pairs there are over 8 million possible combinations in a single gamete (2²³). This is a stretch idea. Fertilisation joins two gametes, giving 46 chromosomes again, and increases variation.

model.problem: A horse body cell has 64 chromosomes. How many chromosomes in (a) a daughter cell after mitosis, (b) a horse gamete, (c) a zygote?

teach.heading: Checks and common errors
bullets: Chromosome number halves only in meiosis
teach.note: Ask pupils to hold up 1 finger for mitosis, 2 for meiosis for each statement read aloud.

misconception.wrong: Meiosis produces gametes identical to each other and to the parent cell.
misconception.right: Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells, each with half the chromosome number.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils recall mitosis for 'growth' but forget gametes need meiosis.

check.q: Which process makes sperm cells in the testes?
check.why: Gametes are made by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number.

practice: How many chromosomes in a human skin cell and sperm cell?
Explain why gametes must be haploid.
State two uses of mitosis.
independent: Core: Make a comparison table of mitosis and meiosis.
Extend: A fruit fly has 8 chromosomes in a body cell. State the number in a gamete and zygote. [2 marks]
Stretch: Explain why siblings (other than identical twins) are not genetically identical. [3 marks]
exit: Define diploid and haploid. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: explain with numbers.
lessons.homework: Draw a diagram of a cell with 4 chromosomes dividing by mitosis and by meiosis.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: chromosome cards to physically sort. Stretch: how does non-disjunction cause Down syndrome?
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Variation and mutation
lessons.bigQuestion: Why are no two people identical, even twins who share all their genes?
objectives: Distinguish genetic and environmental causes of variation
Describe continuous and discontinuous variation
Describe mutation as rare, random and inheritable and state what mutagens are
successCriteria: All: give examples of genetic and environmental variation
Most: describe mutation and mutagens
Some: explain the consequences of a mutation and interpret data
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: data handling and distributions
lessons.smsc: Moral: respect for human difference; avoiding unnecessary exposure to harm

keywords.def: differences between individuals of the same species
random change in the DNA sequence
agent that increases the rate of mutation, e.g. ionising radiation
passed on to offspring if the mutation is in the gametes

starter: Bismillah. Name the molecule that carries genetic information.
State the number of chromosomes in a human gamete.

teach.heading: Causes of variation
bullets: Genetic: different alleles from the parents
Most features are influenced by both
teach.note: Examples: eye colour (genetic), scar (environmental), height (genes plus nutrition), skin tone (genes plus sunlight). Identical twins share genes, so differences between them are environmental. Illustrative class data: height of identical twins differs by about 1 cm, mass by 3 kg.

teach.heading: Mutation
bullets: A mutation changes the base sequence of a gene
Inherited only if it occurs in a gamete or the cell that forms gametes
teach.note: Most mutations are harmless or harmful; a few are beneficial. Mutagens raise the rate: ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, UV) and chemicals in tobacco smoke (Biology only). Link to cancer if mutations affect cell division genes.

model.problem: Explain how a mutation in the gene for an enzyme could stop the enzyme working. [3 marks]
steps: A different amino acid may be placed in the protein chain
The protein folds into a different shape
The active site no longer fits the substrate
model.answer: A changed base sequence can alter the active site shape

teach.heading: Interpreting variation data
bullets: Cause cannot be proved by a correlation alone
teach.note: Give a table of leaf lengths of ivy from sun and shade: e.g. sun mean 4.8 cm, shade mean 6.1 cm. Use as an environmental effect when plants are genetically identical.

misconception.wrong: A mutation is always harmful.
misconception.right: Most are neutral or harmful, but some are beneficial and can spread through a population.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils tick 'hair colour' for environmental because of dye.

check.q: Which is an example of discontinuous variation?
check.why: Blood group falls into distinct categories. Height, mass and foot length vary across a range.

practice: Give one genetic and one environmental cause of variation.
State two mutagens.
Explain why a mutation in a skin cell is not inherited.
independent: Core: Sort ten features into genetic, environmental or both.
Extend: Explain why identical twins raised apart can differ in mass but not blood group. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the statement 'all mutations are harmful'. [4 marks]
exit: Define mutation. [1 mark]
Return to the big question using the terms genes and environment.
lessons.homework: Collect data on a continuous and a discontinuous feature in your family (with permission) and present it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sorting cards with pictures. Stretch: why might a mutation be beneficial in a changing environment?

lessons.title: Natural selection and antibiotic resistance
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a population change over generations, and why do some infections stop responding to treatment?
objectives: Describe Darwin's theory of natural selection in the stages the specification requires
Apply the theory to the peppered moth
Explain how antibiotic resistance develops in bacteria
successCriteria: All: list the stages of natural selection
Most: apply them to a population and to bacteria
Some: explain how data support selection and calculate bacterial growth
lessons.crossCurricular: Medicine: antibiotics; History of science
lessons.smsc: Intellectual honesty: describe the scientific theory accurately as the examination requires, weigh evidence, and respect differing views

keywords.def: process in which better-adapted individuals survive and pass on their alleles more often
feature that helps an organism survive in its environment
ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic
strain of bacteria resistant to many antibiotics

starter: Name the process by which bacteria reproduce.

teach.heading: Darwin's theory: stages
bullets: Individuals in a species show variation
More offspring are born than survive
Better-adapted individuals survive and reproduce, passing on their alleles
teach.note: Be exact: this is what the specification requires pupils to know and explain, and they must use these terms in the exam. Darwin proposed natural selection after observations and the work of others; the modern understanding adds genes and mutation as the source of new alleles. Teach the theory and its supporting evidence precisely; pupils may hold their own views and this lesson is about describing and explaining the scientific theory.
cycle: They reproduce and pass on alleles

teach.heading: Example: peppered moth
bullets: Pale and dark forms of Biston betularia
Industrial areas: soot darkened tree bark
Dark moths survived better; their allele became more common
teach.note: Records from Manchester show dark forms rose from rare in the mid-1800s to about 98% by 1895. After clean-air laws in the 20th century the pale form became common again. Predation by birds acted as the selective pressure.

model.problem: Explain how the dark form of the peppered moth became more common near industrial cities. [4 marks]
steps: There was variation: some moths were dark, some pale
Soot-covered bark made pale moths easier for birds to see
Dark moths survived and reproduced more
They passed on the dark allele, so it became more common
model.answer: Dark moths were better camouflaged, survived and passed on their allele

teach.heading: Antibiotic resistance
bullets: Bacteria vary because of random mutation
Antibiotic kills most bacteria; resistant ones survive
teach.note: Maths: a bacterium divides every 20 minutes. After 2 hours there are 2⁶ = 64 cells; after 6 hours 2¹⁸ = 262 144. Resistance spreads because bacteria multiply quickly. Reduce risk: complete the course, do not use antibiotics for viral infections, avoid overuse.

misconception.wrong: Bacteria become resistant because the antibiotic makes them change on purpose.
misconception.right: Resistant bacteria arise by random mutation. The antibiotic selects them, because the others die.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: 'the bacteria got used to it' is the commonest wrong idea.

check.q: Which statement best explains why a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic?
options: Bacteria learn to resist the drug
The drug causes mutations in all bacteria
Antibiotics make bacteria multiply more slowly
check.why: Random mutation produces some resistant bacteria; the antibiotic kills the rest, so the resistant ones reproduce and pass on the allele.

practice: List the steps of natural selection in order.
State two ways to reduce antibiotic resistance.
Calculate the bacterial number after 3 hours if one cell divides every 20 minutes.
independent: Core: Describe the peppered moth case in five sentences using the terms variation, selection and allele.
Extend: Explain why MRSA is difficult to treat in hospitals. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the evidence for natural selection from the peppered moth. [4 marks]
exit: Define natural selection. [2 marks]
Return to the big question in your own words.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word exam-style explanation of antibiotic resistance.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequence cards of the stages. Stretch: why must people finish an antibiotic course even if they feel well?

lessons.title: Biodiversity, distribution and sampling
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we count the living world, and what does a number of species tell us?
objectives: Define biodiversity and describe how it is measured with quadrats
Estimate a population from quadrat data
Describe how abiotic gradients explain the distribution of organisms along a transect
successCriteria: All: define biodiversity
Most: calculate a population estimate and compare habitats
Some: interpret transect data and evaluate conclusions
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: fieldwork and human impact; Maths: sampling
lessons.smsc: Stewardship (khilafah): protecting the variety of species as an amanah

keywords.def: the number and variety of different species in an area
line across a habitat along which organisms are sampled
choosing sample positions by chance to avoid bias
where organisms are found

teach.heading: Biodiversity
bullets: Species-rich habitats are usually more stable
Damage to a habitat often reduces species number
teach.note: Say clearly: this lesson extends the earlier quadrat lesson to biodiversity (Biology only) and distribution. Contrast a mown lawn (about 3 species) and an unmown meadow (over 12). Link back to food webs: more species gives more feeding links.

teach.heading: Sampling with quadrats
bullets: Place quadrats at random using coordinates
Count each species in every quadrat
Estimate = mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area)
teach.note: Random coordinates from a random number table or generator avoid choosing 'nice' spots. More quadrats make the mean more reliable. Biodiversity is the number of species found.

model.problem: A field has area 600 m². Ten quadrats of 0.25 m² contain these daisy counts: 4, 2, 5, 3, 6, 4, 3, 5, 2, 6. Estimate the population of daisies.

teach.heading: Distribution along a transect
bullets: Lay a tape from woodland edge into open grass
Quadrat every 5 m; measure light each time
Compare abundance with the abiotic factor
teach.note: Sample data: distance 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 m; shade-loving fern per m²: 22, 15, 8, 2, 0; relative light: 12, 25, 48, 80, 100. Pattern: fern decreases as light rises. Correlation suggests but does not prove cause; check soil moisture and pH as well.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils pick a link as proof; other abiotic factors might also change along the transect.

check.q: Fern numbers fall as light increases along a transect. What is the best conclusion?
options: Light could be a factor, but other factors should be checked
Ferns cannot live in the light
check.why: Correlation is not proof of cause. Moisture, soil and temperature may also vary along the transect.

practice: Define biodiversity.
Why are quadrat positions chosen at random?
A field of 400 m² has a mean of 5 plants per 1 m² quadrat. Estimate the population.
independent: Core: Calculate the mean and population estimate from the data your teacher gives for a 0.5 m² quadrat.
Extend: Explain why the meadow has higher biodiversity than the lawn. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate how reliable your fern conclusion is and suggest two improvements. [4 marks]
exit: State two ways to make quadrat data more reliable. [2 marks]
Return to the big question in one sentence.
lessons.homework: Plan a biodiversity survey of a school garden: method, variables and a risk assessment.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: photographs of species with name cards. Stretch: name another measure such as an index of diversity.

lessons.title: Crop yield, pest control and fish farming
lessons.bigQuestion: How can farmers grow more food without wasting the Earth's resources?
objectives: Explain how glasshouses, polythene tunnels, carbon dioxide, temperature, fertilisers and pest control increase crop yield
Compare chemical and biological pest control
Describe fish-farming methods and their problems (Biology only)
successCriteria: All: list ways to raise crop yield
Most: explain reasons and compare pest control
Some: evaluate cost and environmental impact using data
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: food security; Economics: cost-benefit
lessons.smsc: Stewardship: using resources without waste (israf); providing halal and tayyib food

keywords.def: amount of crop produced per unit area
using a living organism to control a pest
substance supplying mineral ions to plants
number of fish per unit volume of water

starter: Bismillah. Name three limiting factors of photosynthesis.
What do plants use nitrate for?

teach.heading: Raising crop yield
bullets: Glasshouses and polythene tunnels keep warmth, light and humidity
Extra CO₂ and warmth speed photosynthesis
Fertilisers (N, P, K) supply mineral ions
teach.note: Link to limiting factors. A glasshouse traps heat and shelters from wind and pests. Some growers burn paraffin for heat and CO₂. Nitrates make amino acids, phosphates help roots and energy transfer, potassium helps enzymes.

teach.heading: Model: evaluate using data
teach.note: Value: field 6 × 2 = £12, glasshouse 22 × 2 = £44, glasshouse + CO₂ 28 × 2 = £56. Profit after cost: £10.50, £36.00, £46.50. Real farms also count energy use and carbon footprint.

model.problem: Using the table and tomatoes selling at £2 per kg, calculate the profit per m² for the glasshouse with CO₂ and compare with the open field.
steps: Glasshouse + CO₂ profit is about 4.4 times greater
model.answer: £46.50 per m², about 4.4 times the field profit

teach.heading: Pest control and fish farming
bullets: Pesticides kill pests but can harm other organisms
Biological control: ladybirds eat aphids; no chemical residue
Fish farms: control predators, disease, water quality, feeding
teach.note: Chemical: fast but can spread through food chains and pests may evolve resistance. Biological: slower, specific, but the agent may become a pest itself. Fish farming (Biology only): benefits include protecting wild stocks and reliable supply; problems include waste and uneaten food polluting water, disease and parasites spreading to wild fish, escaped fish breeding with wild fish, and fishmeal from wild catch.

left.title: Chemical pesticide
points: May build up in food chains

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils think the biggest yield is always best; cost and environmental effects matter.

check.q: Which is a disadvantage of using chemical pesticides?
options: They may harm useful insects and enter food chains
check.why: Pesticides can kill non-target organisms such as bees and can be passed along food chains.

practice: State two ways a glasshouse increases yield.
Why can fertiliser run-off cause problems?
Give one problem of fish farming.
independent: Core: Make a table of advantages and disadvantages of biological control.
Extend: Explain why adding CO₂ to a glasshouse increases yield only if light and temperature are high enough. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the use of a glasshouse and chemical pesticide for producing tomatoes in the UK. [4 marks]
exit: Name three factors a grower can control in a glasshouse. [3 marks]
Return to the big question: balance yield and the environment in two sentences.
lessons.homework: Write a short plan for a school glasshouse to grow cucumbers, justifying each control.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pictures of glasshouse controls. Stretch: calculate cost-benefit if CO₂ enrichment costs £3 more.

lessons.title: Yeast, Lactobacillus and industrial fermenters
lessons.bigQuestion: How can tiny organisms make bread, yoghurt and medicines?
objectives: Describe the use of yeast in bread making and Lactobacillus in yoghurt
Describe the structure and conditions of an industrial fermenter
Explain the need for aseptic conditions
successCriteria: All: name the organisms and products
Most: describe the conditions of a fermenter
Some: explain why each condition is controlled
lessons.crossCurricular: Food technology: baking and dairy; Chemistry: fermentation
lessons.smsc: Gratitude for provision; careful, clean food preparation (tahara, tayyib)

keywords.def: vessel for growing microorganisms on a large scale
free from unwanted microorganisms
acid made by Lactobacillus when fermenting lactose
protein-rich food made from a fungus

starter: Bismillah. Write the equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
State the optimum conditions for enzymes.
Name the gas that makes bread rise.

teach.heading: Bread and yoghurt
bullets: Yeast respires sugar, releasing CO₂ to make dough rise
Ethanol evaporates when the bread is baked
Lactobacillus changes lactose into lactic acid
teach.note: Yoghurt method: heat milk to about 72 °C for 15 seconds to kill unwanted microbes, cool to about 43 °C, add Lactobacillus starter culture, incubate for several hours. The falling pH makes milk protein clot, thickening and giving the sour taste.
cycle: Heat milk to kill unwanted microbes
Lactic acid thickens the milk into yoghurt

teach.heading: The industrial fermenter
bullets: Stirrer mixes; water jacket removes heat
teach.note: Fermenters make antibiotics such as penicillin (from the fungus Penicillium) and mycoprotein (from the fungus Fusarium). Respiration releases heat, so cooling is necessary. A stirrer spreads nutrients and oxygen and keeps temperature even.

head: Control
Reason
rows: even mixing of nutrients and heat

teach.heading: Model: explain controls
teach.note: Practice phrase: conditions, enzymes, optimum, yield. Contamination can ruin a whole batch costing thousands of pounds.

model.problem: Explain why a fermenter has a water jacket and a stirrer. [4 marks]
steps: Respiration releases heat, which could denature enzymes
The water jacket removes heat to keep optimum temperature
The stirrer mixes nutrients and oxygen through the culture
So all microorganisms get nutrients and growth is fast
model.answer: Cooling keeps enzymes working and stirring spreads nutrients and oxygen

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils think Lactobacillus uses glucose to make ethanol; it produces lactic acid.

check.q: Which organism and product are used to make yoghurt?
check.why: Lactobacillus ferments lactose into lactic acid, which thickens milk.

practice: Name the organism used in bread making.
Why is milk heated before making yoghurt?
State two controlled conditions in a fermenter.
independent: Core: Draw and label a fermenter with five features.
Extend: Explain why sterile air is pumped into a fermenter used for penicillin. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate making food protein using a fungus compared with raising animals. [4 marks]
exit: State why aseptic conditions are needed. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: pick one product and explain the process.
lessons.homework: Make a flow chart of yoghurt production with controlled conditions beside each step.

lessons.title: Selective breeding of plants and animals
lessons.bigQuestion: How did one wild plant become cabbage, broccoli and cauliflower?
objectives: Describe the process of selective breeding
Give examples of traits selected in crops and animals
Evaluate the benefits and problems
successCriteria: All: describe the steps
Most: give examples and benefits
Some: explain reduced genetic diversity and evaluate
lessons.crossCurricular: History: early agriculture; Economics: farming
lessons.smsc: Stewardship: caring for animals with kindness while meeting human needs

keywords.def: choosing parents with desired traits to breed over generations
characteristic
breeding closely related individuals
range of alleles in a population

starter: State the difference between a gene and an allele.

teach.heading: The process
bullets: Choose parents with the desired trait
Breed them and select the best offspring
teach.note: Choice is made by humans (artificial selection), unlike natural selection. Examples: cows with high milk yield, wheat with disease resistance, dogs with certain temperaments, crops with larger fruit, hens with more eggs.

teach.heading: Example: milk yield
bullets: Average yield per cow has risen steeply
Yield about 4000 litres a year in the 1970s
Over 7500 litres a year today (UK average, approximate)
teach.note: Part of the rise is better feeding and care; selection for milk yield also contributed. Ask: what might the cow's welfare costs be? (more lameness, udder infections).

model.problem: Describe how a farmer could produce a variety of wheat with high yield and resistance to a fungal disease. [4 marks]
steps: Choose wheat plants with the highest yield and plants resistant to the disease
Grow the seeds and select offspring that show both traits

teach.heading: Benefits and drawbacks
bullets: Benefit: higher yield, better quality, disease resistance
Inbreeding can increase harmful recessive disorders
teach.note: Real example: the Irish potato famine of the 1840s involved a heavily clonal, near-uniform potato crop affected by blight. A population with little variation may have no resistant individuals when a new disease arrives.

misconception.wrong: Selective breeding is genetic engineering.
misconception.right: In selective breeding whole organisms with desired alleles are bred over generations. Genetic engineering moves specific genes directly.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils say the cow changes during its life; selection acts across generations.

check.q: Which is a problem of selective breeding?
options: Offspring are completely different from parents
check.why: Repeated selection from a small group lowers variation, so a disease can affect the whole population.

practice: Define selective breeding.
Give two traits that may be selected in cattle.
Why is it slower than genetic engineering?
independent: Core: Write the steps of selective breeding for tomatoes with bigger fruit.
Extend: Explain how selective breeding differs from natural selection. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate whether selective breeding of dogs for appearance is acceptable. [4 marks]
exit: State one benefit and one drawback of selective breeding. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: explain it in three steps.
lessons.homework: Research one crop or animal that has been selectively bred and summarise the changes.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: before/after pictures of crops. Stretch: how does inbreeding increase recessive disorders?

lessons.title: Genetic engineering and human insulin
lessons.bigQuestion: How can bacteria be programmed to make human medicine?
objectives: Describe the steps of genetic engineering
Explain the roles of restriction enzymes, ligase and vectors
Describe how GM bacteria make human insulin
successCriteria: All: define genetic engineering
Most: sequence the steps and name enzymes
Some: explain the benefits and issues of GM insulin
lessons.crossCurricular: Medicine: diabetes; Chemistry: enzymes
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing benefit and risk; responsibility in applying science for healing

keywords.def: changing an organism's genes by moving DNA from one organism to another
enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific sequence
enzyme that joins DNA pieces together
carrier (plasmid or virus) used to transfer DNA into cells

starter: What is an enzyme's active site?

teach.heading: The steps
bullets: Cut the human insulin gene out with a restriction enzyme
Cut a plasmid with the same enzyme
Join the gene into the plasmid with ligase
Grow the bacteria in a fermenter
teach.note: Restriction enzymes leave 'sticky ends' that match; ligase seals the joins. Viruses can also be vectors. Bacteria then copy the plasmid and make insulin. Extract and purify.
cycle: Insert into a plasmid with ligase
Bacteria make insulin in a fermenter

teach.heading: Why GM insulin
bullets: Insulin controls blood glucose in diabetes
Previously extracted from pig and cow pancreases
GM human insulin is cheaper, plentiful, and suits more patients
teach.note: GM insulin was first approved in the early 1980s. Bacteria reproduce quickly in fermenters, so supply is large.

model.problem: Explain the roles of restriction enzymes and ligase in making GM bacteria. [4 marks]
steps: Restriction enzyme cuts DNA at a specific base sequence
It cuts both the gene and plasmid, leaving sticky ends
Ligase joins the gene into the plasmid backbone
This makes a recombinant plasmid that bacteria can take up
model.answer: Restriction enzymes cut; ligase joins; the plasmid carries the gene

teach.heading: Plasmid or virus as vector
bullets: A vector carries DNA into a cell
Viruses insert their genetic material into host cells
teach.note: Link to bacteria: plasmids are small circles of DNA in addition to the main chromosome.

misconception.wrong: Genetic engineering and selective breeding are the same thing.
misconception.right: Genetic engineering moves specific genes directly using enzymes and vectors. Selective breeding works across generations by choosing parents.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: confusing restriction enzyme with ligase because both 'work on DNA'.

check.q: Which enzyme joins a gene into a plasmid?
check.why: Ligase joins DNA fragments. Restriction enzymes cut DNA.

practice: List the steps to produce GM bacteria for insulin.
What is a vector?
Name the enzyme that cuts DNA.
independent: Core: Draw the steps of genetic engineering using a flow chart.
Extend: Explain why bacteria are used to make human insulin. [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the benefits and risks of genetic engineering in medicine. [4 marks]
exit: Define genetic engineering. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: describe in a sentence how bacteria become insulin factories.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph explaining GM insulin to a person with diabetes.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: step cards with diagrams. Stretch: how can the gene be made from mRNA?

lessons.title: Transgenic organisms, GM crops and cloning
lessons.bigQuestion: Should we move genes between species, and can we copy a whole animal?
objectives: Describe transgenic organisms and GM crops with examples
Evaluate benefits and concerns of GM food production
Describe micropropagation and nuclear transfer including Dolly the sheep (Biology only)
successCriteria: All: define transgenic and cloning
Most: describe examples and the Dolly process
Some: evaluate GM crops and cloning from several perspectives
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: food security; Ethics
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing benefit, risk, justice and care for creation; respect for different considered views

keywords.def: containing a gene from a different species
growing many plants from small pieces of tissue in sterile culture
putting a nucleus from a body cell into an egg cell with its nucleus removed
genetically identical organism

teach.heading: GM crops
bullets: Transgenic plants carry a gene from another species
Golden rice: genes for beta-carotene (makes vitamin A)
Bt crops: bacterial gene gives resistance to insect pests
teach.note: Golden rice was developed to help reduce vitamin A deficiency. Bt maize and cotton contain a toxin gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. Herbicide-resistant crops are also grown. State both advantages and the controversy fairly.

teach.heading: Micropropagation
bullets: Take tiny pieces from the shoot tip
Grow on sterile nutrient agar with plant hormones
teach.note: Used for orchids and banana plants. Advantages: many identical plants quickly, disease-free stock. Disadvantages: expensive, plants are genetically identical.

teach.heading: Dolly the sheep: nuclear transfer
bullets: Nucleus from an adult udder cell of a Finn Dorset sheep
Placed into an egg cell with its nucleus removed
Dolly born in 1996, genetically identical to the donor
teach.note: The egg came from a Scottish Blackface ewe; the surrogate was also a Scottish Blackface. An electric pulse made the cell divide. Dolly lived to age 6; discuss welfare and the ethical debate respectfully.

model.problem: Describe how Dolly was produced. [4 marks]
steps: A nucleus was removed from an unfertilised egg cell
The nucleus from a udder cell of another sheep was inserted
The cell was stimulated to divide, making an embryo
The embryo was implanted into a surrogate mother
model.answer: Nuclear transfer into an enucleated egg, then implantation

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Dolly was not made by fertilisation
The DNA came from one donor
teach.note: Ask: which parent does Dolly resemble? (the udder-cell donor).

misconception.wrong: Dolly was produced by fertilising an egg with sperm in a laboratory.
misconception.right: Dolly came from nuclear transfer, with no sperm. She was genetically identical to the donor of the nucleus.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: transgenic means a gene from another species, not any genetic change.

check.q: A plant with a gene from a bacterium is:
check.why: Transgenic organisms contain a gene from a different species.

practice: Define transgenic.
State two advantages of micropropagation.
Why is Dolly genetically identical to the sheep that donated the nucleus?
independent: Core: Make a table of benefits and risks of GM crops.
Extend: Explain why plants produced by micropropagation are at risk from a single disease. [3 marks]
Stretch: Discuss whether human societies should clone farm animals. [5 marks]
exit: Describe the stages of micropropagation. [3 marks]
Return to the big question: present one view for and one against with evidence.
lessons.homework: Write a balanced 150-word evaluation of GM crops.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: diagrams with caption matching. Stretch: how are mitochondria DNA inherited in Dolly?

lessons.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions and calorimetry
lessons.bigQuestion: How much energy does a reaction release, and how can you measure it with a cup and a thermometer?
objectives: Distinguish exothermic and endothermic reactions with examples
Use Q = m × c × ΔT
Calculate molar enthalpy change from calorimetry data
successCriteria: All: classify reactions by temperature change
Most: calculate Q
Some: calculate molar enthalpy change and evaluate the method
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: energy transfer; Food technology: hand warmers
lessons.smsc: Stewardship: understanding energy use and heat loss

keywords.def: reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings; temperature rises
reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings; temperature falls
energy change in a reaction measured in kJ/mol
measuring energy changes by the temperature change of water

starter: Bismillah. State the specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J/g/°C).
Calculate moles in 4.0 g of NaOH (Mr 40).

teach.heading: Exo and endo
bullets: Energy is conserved; it moves between system and surroundings
teach.note: Examples: exothermic: combustion, neutralisation, respiration, metals in acid; endothermic: thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, photosynthesis, citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Practical: measure temperature change when sodium hydroxide neutralises hydrochloric acid, and when ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, in a polystyrene cup with a lid. Safety: goggles; corrosive solutions.

teach.heading: Calorimetry: Q = m c ΔT
bullets: Q = energy in J; m = mass of water in g
c = 4.18 J/g/°C; ΔT = change in temperature
Molar enthalpy: ΔH = −Q ÷ moles (in J then kJ/mol)
teach.note: Treat 1 cm³ of dilute solution as 1 g. Exothermic ΔH is negative. Use sign to match the temperature change.

model.problem: 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl and 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ NaOH are mixed. The temperature rises by 6.5 °C. Calculate Q and the molar enthalpy change of neutralisation.

teach.heading: Evaluating the experiment
teach.note: Because heat is lost, the measured temperature rise is smaller and the ΔH is less negative than the data book. For combustion of ethanol with a spirit burner, heat loss is much larger: 0.46 g ethanol heating 100 g water by 25 °C gives −1045 kJ/mol against a data book value of about −1367 kJ/mol.

misconception.wrong: In an exothermic reaction the reaction gets cold because energy is lost.
misconception.right: The reaction releases energy to the surroundings, so the surroundings (and the thermometer) get hotter.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils use the total volume of mixture mass incorrectly or miss the minus sign.

check.q: A reaction in water raises the temperature of 100 g of water by 10 °C. What is Q? (c = 4.18 J/g/°C)

practice: Classify: respiration, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate.
Calculate Q for 200 g of water rising by 8.0 °C.
State why a lid is used on the cup.
independent: Core: Describe the practical to measure the temperature change on neutralisation.
Extend: 0.46 g ethanol (Mr 46) heats 100 g water by 25 °C. Calculate the molar enthalpy change. [4 marks]
Stretch: Give three reasons the answer for ethanol is lower than the data book and suggest improvements. [4 marks]
exit: Define exothermic and endothermic. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: describe how you would measure the energy of a reaction.
lessons.homework: Write a method for finding the energy change on dissolving a salt, with a table of results.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: formula triangle for Q; practice with small numbers. Stretch: compare the enthalpy values of different fuels.

lessons.title: Energy level diagrams and bond energies
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does breaking bonds take energy but making them give it out?
objectives: Draw and interpret energy level diagrams
Explain energy changes in terms of bond breaking and making
Calculate ΔH from bond energies
successCriteria: All: identify exo and endothermic from a diagram
Most: explain bond breaking and making
Some: calculate ΔH from bond energy data
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: energy conservation
lessons.smsc: Reflection: energy is conserved and transformed (amanah in use of resources)

keywords.def: energy needed to break one mole of a given bond
minimum energy needed for reaction
graph of energy of reactants and products
overall energy change

starter: Write the equation for methane burning.

teach.heading: Energy level diagrams
bullets: ΔH is the difference in energy
teach.note: Draw both on the board. Label energy axis and progress of reaction. In reaction profile diagrams a hump shows the activation energy.

teach.heading: Bond breaking and making
teach.note: Use data: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432 kJ/mol. Check signs carefully; pupils often subtract the wrong way.

model.problem: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432 kJ/mol. Calculate ΔH.

teach.heading: A second example: methane
teach.note: Data: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464. Break: 4 × 413 + 2 × 498 = 2648. Make: 2 × 805 + 4 × 464 = 3466. ΔH = −818 kJ/mol. Why is the result not exactly the same as data book values? Bond energies are averages.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils reverse the subtraction and give a positive value.

check.q: Energy to break bonds is 800 kJ and energy released making bonds is 950 kJ. What is ΔH?
check.why: ΔH = 800 − 950 = −150 kJ. The reaction is exothermic.

practice: Sketch an exothermic energy level diagram.
State whether breaking bonds is endothermic or exothermic.
Calculate ΔH if bonds broken = 1200 kJ and bonds made = 1000 kJ.
independent: Core: Use bond energies to calculate ΔH for H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr (H–H 436, Br–Br 193, H–Br 366).
Extend: Calculate ΔH for the combustion of hydrogen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (H–H 436, O=O 498, O–H 464). [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why bond energy calculations are only approximate. [2 marks]
exit: Define activation energy. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: link bond breaking, bond making and ΔH.
lessons.homework: Complete three bond-energy calculations and draw their energy diagrams.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: step table for calculation (broken, made, difference). Stretch: effect of a catalyst on the diagram.

lessons.title: Rates of reaction and collision theory
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a crushed tablet dissolve faster, and food spoil faster in the heat?
objectives: Describe how concentration, surface area, pressure and temperature affect rate
Explain each factor using collision theory
Describe and analyse the marble chips and acid investigation
successCriteria: All: list the factors that change rate
Most: explain using collision theory
Some: calculate rates and interpret graphs
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: enzymes; Food science: preservation
lessons.smsc: Moral: waste reduction by understanding spoilage

keywords.def: how fast reactants are used or products formed
particles must collide with enough energy to react
total area of solid exposed to reactants
minimum energy for a successful collision

starter: Bismillah. Write the equation for calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid.
State the volume of 1 mol of gas.

teach.heading: Collision theory
bullets: In the right orientation; successful collisions give a reaction
teach.note: Increase the frequency of successful collisions to raise the rate. Use particle diagrams.

head: Factor
Change
Effect on collisions
rows: more particles per volume, more collisions
faster particles: more collisions and more with energy above activation energy

teach.heading: Marble chips practical
bullets: Measure CO₂ volume or loss of mass over time
Change one factor, e.g. chip size
teach.note: Variables: independent chip size; dependent volume of gas every 20 s; control acid concentration, volume, mass of chips, temperature. A gas syringe or an upturned measuring cylinder over water works; or use a balance with cotton wool in the flask neck. Safety: goggles; spill risk. Use sodium thiosulfate with HCl for temperature; time for a cross to disappear; rate = 1 ÷ time.

teach.heading: Model: using the data
bullets: Both finish at the same volume: same mass of CaCO₃
teach.note: Large chips take 100 s to reach 30 cm³: mean rate 0.30 cm³/s. Small chips take 60 s: mean rate 0.50 cm³/s. Initial rates (0–20 s): 0.50 and 0.90 cm³/s.

model.problem: Using the table, calculate the mean rate for each size of chip and explain the difference.
steps: Small chips have a greater surface area
More collisions per second, so a faster rate
model.answer: 0.30 and 0.50 cm³/s; greater surface area gives more frequent collisions

teach.heading: Temperature and collisions
bullets: A greater proportion have energy above the activation energy
teach.note: Both effects matter, the second is bigger. Pupils usually give only the first. Rule of thumb: a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate for many reactions.

misconception.wrong: Temperature increases the rate only because particles collide more often.
misconception.right: Collisions are more frequent and, more importantly, more of them have energy above the activation energy.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: 'more collisions' alone is incomplete for temperature.

check.q: Why does increasing temperature increase the rate of reaction?
options: Collisions are more frequent and more have energy above activation energy
check.why: Faster particles collide more often and a greater proportion have enough energy. Activation energy is unchanged by temperature.

practice: List four factors that affect reaction rate.
Explain why powdered marble reacts faster than lumps.
Calculate the mean rate: 40 cm³ in 80 s.
independent: Core: Plot the data and add curves for large and small chips.
Extend: Sketch the graph for the same reaction at higher temperature and explain. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why increasing pressure increases rate for gases but not liquids. [3 marks]
exit: State what collision theory says. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: explain one everyday example.
lessons.homework: Explain in 100 words why food spoils faster in summer using collision theory.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: particle diagrams for each factor. Stretch: use the initial gradient to find the initial rate.

lessons.title: Catalysts and reaction profiles
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a substance speed up a reaction without being used up?
objectives: Describe how a catalyst works
Draw and interpret reaction profile diagrams (Chemistry only)
Describe an investigation of catalysts with hydrogen peroxide
successCriteria: All: describe a catalyst
Most: sketch a reaction profile with and without a catalyst
Some: calculate activation energy and ΔH from a profile
lessons.crossCurricular: Industry: catalytic converters; Biology: enzymes
lessons.smsc: Stewardship: catalysts reduce energy use and pollution

keywords.def: substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up
minimum energy needed for a collision to react
energy diagram showing the path from reactants to products
different route with lower Ea

starter: State how surface area affects rate.

teach.heading: What a catalyst does
bullets: Provides an alternative pathway with a lower Ea
Not used up; may be reused; can be specific
teach.note: Examples: manganese(IV) oxide for hydrogen peroxide; iron in the Haber process; platinum and rhodium in catalytic converters; enzymes in cells. A catalyst does not change the products or ΔH.

head: Catalyst
Reaction
rows: pollutant gases in a car exhaust

teach.heading: Reaction profiles
bullets: Reactants at one level, products at another
A catalyst lowers the peak; ΔH unchanged
teach.note: Draw the diagram and mark Ea and ΔH. Example data: reactants at 0 kJ, peak +150 kJ, products at −80 kJ; Ea = 150 kJ, ΔH = −80 kJ. With a catalyst the peak is +70 kJ: Ea = 70 kJ; ΔH remains −80 kJ.

model.problem: A reaction profile has reactants at 0 kJ, a peak at +150 kJ and products at −80 kJ. A catalyst lowers the peak to +70 kJ. State Ea and ΔH with and without the catalyst.
model.answer: Ea 150 → 70 kJ; ΔH = −80 kJ in both cases

teach.heading: Practical: hydrogen peroxide
bullets: Measure oxygen volume in a gas syringe every 20 s
Keep mass of catalyst, volume and concentration of peroxide the same
teach.note: Data: with MnO₂, 60 cm³ in 40 s (1.5 cm³/s); with CuO, 40 cm³ in 80 s (0.50 cm³/s); no catalyst only 4 cm³ in 120 s (0.03 cm³/s). Recover the catalyst by filtering, drying and weighing: the mass is unchanged. Safety: goggles; hydrogen peroxide can bleach skin.

misconception.wrong: A catalyst gives the reactants extra energy so the reaction goes faster.
misconception.right: A catalyst gives a different pathway with a lower activation energy; the energy of reactants and products does not change.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils think the catalyst changes ΔH or is used up.

check.q: What effect does a catalyst have on a reaction?
check.why: A catalyst lowers the activation energy; ΔH and the products are unchanged.

practice: State what a catalyst is.
Name the catalyst for hydrogen peroxide decomposition.
State how you would show the catalyst is not used up.
independent: Core: Sketch a reaction profile with and without a catalyst for an exothermic reaction.
Extend: Using the data, rank the catalysts and calculate their mean rates. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why enzymes are often described as highly specific catalysts. [3 marks]
exit: Define catalyst. [1 mark]
Return to the big question using activation energy.
lessons.homework: Annotate two reaction profiles: one exothermic, one endothermic, each with and without catalyst.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn axes to label. Stretch: why is platinum used in catalytic converters?

lessons.title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
lessons.bigQuestion: Can a reaction run backwards, and when do forward and backward reactions balance?
objectives: Describe reversible reactions with examples
Describe dynamic equilibrium (Chemistry only)
Predict the effect of temperature and pressure on the position of equilibrium
successCriteria: All: use the reversible symbol with examples
Most: describe dynamic equilibrium
Some: predict changes in position and apply to the Haber process
lessons.crossCurricular: Industry: ammonia and fertiliser; Biology: haemoglobin
lessons.smsc: Stewardship: efficient industry reduces energy waste

keywords.def: reaction that can go in both directions, shown by ⇌
forward and backward rates equal; concentrations constant
relative amounts of reactants and products
no substances enter or leave

starter: Name the product of the Haber process.

teach.heading: Reversible reactions
bullets: Hydrated copper sulfate: blue ⇌ white + water
teach.note: Heat blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate: it turns white, water is driven off; add water and it turns blue again, getting warm. One direction is endothermic, the reverse is exothermic by the same amount of energy.

teach.heading: Dynamic equilibrium
bullets: In a closed system the rates become equal
Reactions are still happening in both directions
teach.note: Use the analogy of an escalator with people walking down at the same rate as it carries them up: the person stays at the same height, but is still moving. Equilibrium is reached only in a closed system.

teach.heading: Changing conditions
bullets: Higher temperature favours the endothermic direction
Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles
Catalysts do not change the position
teach.note: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic forwards, with 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. High pressure moves the position to the right; high temperature moves it left but speeds up the rate. Industrial compromise: about 450 °C, 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst.

model.problem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is exothermic. Predict and explain the effect of increased pressure and of higher temperature on the yield of ammonia.
steps: Left side 4 moles of gas, right side 2 moles
Higher pressure favours fewer moles, so more ammonia
Higher temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, so less ammonia
model.answer: More ammonia at higher pressure; less at higher temperature

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: 'nothing is happening' is the typical misconception of dynamic equilibrium.

check.q: In a dynamic equilibrium:
options: Forward and backward rates are equal
check.why: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations are constant (not necessarily equal).

practice: Write the equation for hydrated copper sulfate as a reversible reaction.
Why must the system be closed?
Which side has fewer gas moles in N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃?
independent: Core: Describe how to show that heating blue copper sulfate is reversible.
Extend: In N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ the mixture turns darker when heated. Is the forward reaction exothermic or endothermic? Explain. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why industry uses a compromise temperature in the Haber process. [4 marks]
exit: Define dynamic equilibrium. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: where does the 'dynamic' come from?

lessons.title: Naming organic compounds, functional groups and isomers
lessons.bigQuestion: How can one molecular formula describe more than one real substance?
objectives: Name alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids with up to six carbons
Identify functional groups
Draw and name isomers
successCriteria: All: name straight-chain alkanes and alkenes
Most: name using the functional group and position
Some: draw and name all isomers of C₅H₁₂ and C₄H₈
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: systematic naming; Biology: biological molecules
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: order in naming, as in all branches of knowledge

keywords.def: atom or group giving a compound its characteristic reactions
compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures
internationally agreed system for naming compounds
formula showing how the atoms are arranged, e.g. CH₃CH₂CH₃

starter: State the general formula of alkanes.

teach.heading: Stems and functional groups
bullets: Stems: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6
Alkene: C=C, ends -ene; alcohol -OH, -ol; acid -COOH, -oic acid
teach.note: Earlier lessons covered hydrocarbon formulae and homologous series; this lesson focuses on naming and isomers (including positions of double bonds). Position numbers are required for chains from C₄ up (but-1-ene, but-2-ene).

teach.heading: Model: naming a branched alkane
bullets: Number from the end giving lowest numbers
teach.note: Example CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃: the longest chain is 3 carbons (propane) with one methyl branch at carbon 2, so 2-methylpropane. Write structural formulae in text if no diagram is available.

model.problem: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
steps: One CH₃ branch on carbon 2 (count from either end: the lowest is 2)

teach.heading: Isomers
teach.note: C₅H₁₂ has three isomers: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane. Isomers have different physical properties, such as boiling points (branched isomers boil at lower temperature).

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils call all C₄H₁₀ drawings different when they are the same chain bent differently.

check.q: Which pair are isomers?
check.why: Both are C₄H₁₀ with different structures. The other pairs have different molecular formulae.

practice: Name the alkane with 5 carbons and the alkene with 4 carbons.
Write the structural formula for propan-1-ol.
Name CH₃CH₂COOH.
independent: Core: Draw and name the isomers of C₄H₁₀.
Extend: Draw and name all isomers of C₅H₁₂. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why but-1-ene and but-2-ene are isomers but ethene and propene are not. [2 marks]
exit: Define isomers. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: show one formula with two names.
lessons.homework: Complete a naming worksheet for 10 compounds (alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, acids).
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: stem cards (meth, eth, prop...). Stretch: name a branched alkene.

lessons.title: Alcohols: manufacture, oxidation and uses
lessons.bigQuestion: Ethanol can come from sugar cane or from crude oil: which source is better?
objectives: Describe the structure and combustion of alcohols
Compare manufacture of ethanol by fermentation and by hydration of ethene
Describe oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid
successCriteria: All: state the functional group and an example
Most: compare the two manufacturing methods
Some: evaluate the methods and write equations
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: biofuels; Economics: sustainability
lessons.smsc: Moral: ethanol is used industrially as fuel and solvent; drinking alcohol is prohibited in Islam, and the lesson discusses industrial chemistry only

keywords.def: organic compound containing the –OH group
anaerobic respiration of glucose by yeast producing ethanol
adding water, e.g. to ethene
here, converting an alcohol to a carboxylic acid

starter: Bismillah. Name the functional group of alkenes.
What is anaerobic respiration in yeast?

teach.heading: Alcohols
bullets: Burn to form CO₂ and H₂O
teach.note: Combustion: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. Uses: fuels, solvents, antiseptics, industrial feedstock. Higher alcohols are less volatile.

teach.heading: Two ways to make ethanol
bullets: Hydration uses 300 °C, 60–70 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst
teach.note: Fermentation uses yeast at about 30 °C without air, then fractional distillation to concentrate. Hydration uses steam and ethene from cracked crude oil in a continuous process.

teach.heading: Model: evaluating methods
teach.note: Frame the answer: one advantage, one disadvantage for each, then a conclusion tied to context (e.g. a country with plentiful sugar cane and little oil).

model.problem: A country has a lot of sugar cane but no oil. Evaluate fermentation for making ethanol fuel there. [4 marks]
steps: Sugar cane is a local renewable raw material
Fermentation needs low temperature, so energy costs are lower
It is a slow batch process and gives dilute ethanol needing distillation
Overall suitable because raw materials are cheap and renewable
model.answer: Fermentation suits that country: local renewable feedstock and lower energy use

teach.heading: Oxidation of ethanol
bullets: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) turns orange to green
Ethanol solutions left open become vinegar by microbial oxidation
teach.note: Oxidation by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI): ethanol → ethanoic acid. Safety: dichromate is toxic and carcinogenic (teacher demonstration).

misconception.wrong: Ethanol is made only by fermentation.
misconception.right: Ethanol is made by fermentation and by hydration of ethene.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: confusing fermentation conditions with hydration conditions.

check.q: Which is an advantage of making ethanol by fermentation?
options: It is a fast continuous process
It uses a renewable raw material
It uses high temperature and pressure
check.why: Fermentation uses renewable sugar from plants. It is slower and gives dilute product.

practice: Write the equation for the combustion of ethanol.
State the catalyst in hydration of ethene.
What colour change shows oxidation by acidified dichromate(VI)?
independent: Core: Make a table comparing fermentation and hydration of ethene.
Extend: Write the equation for fermentation and calculate the mass of ethanol from 90 g glucose (Mr glucose 180, ethanol 46). [3 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate whether producing ethanol fuel from sugar cane is sustainable. [4 marks]
exit: Name the functional group in alcohols. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: choose a source and justify it.
lessons.homework: Write a risk assessment for burning alcohols in a spirit burner.

lessons.title: Carboxylic acids and esters
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does the smell of pear drops and perfume come from?
objectives: Describe the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids
Describe how esters are made from alcohols and acids
Describe the practical preparation of an ester
successCriteria: All: name acids and describe their reactions
Most: write the equation for ester formation
Some: name esters and evaluate the preparation method
lessons.crossCurricular: Food technology: flavourings; Chemistry: acids
lessons.smsc: Moral: safe handling in preparation; observation and care

keywords.def: organic compound containing –COOH
compound formed from an alcohol and carboxylic acid; contains –COO–
acid that is only partially ionised in water
reaction of an alcohol with a carboxylic acid to form an ester and water

starter: Bismillah. Name the functional group in alcohols.
State the products of an acid with a carbonate.

teach.heading: Carboxylic acids
bullets: Weak acids; ethanoic acid pH about 3 (0.1 mol/dm³)
React with metals, carbonates, alkalis like other acids
teach.note: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ is only partly ionised. Compare 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl (pH 1) with ethanoic acid (pH 3) and note fizzing with magnesium is slower. Reaction: 2CH₃COOH + Mg → (CH₃COO)₂Mg + H₂; with sodium carbonate they give CO₂.

teach.heading: Making esters
teach.note: Naming: the alcohol part gives the first word (ethyl), the acid gives the second (ethanoate). Practical: 2 cm³ ethanol, 2 cm³ ethanoic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid in a test tube; warm in a hot-water bath for about 5 minutes (no naked flames: ethanol is flammable); pour into sodium carbonate solution to neutralise excess acid; smell carefully by wafting. Safety: goggles; concentrated acid is corrosive.

model.problem: Write the name and equation for the ester formed from methanol and ethanoic acid.
steps: Alcohol part: methyl; acid part: ethanoate
model.answer: Methyl ethanoate: CH₃COOH + CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O

teach.heading: Properties and uses
bullets: Volatile, insoluble or slightly soluble in water
teach.note: Pear drops contain an ester called pentyl ethanoate (amyl acetate). Naming more esters: ethyl methanoate, propyl ethanoate.

misconception.wrong: Esters form from two acids reacting together.
misconception.right: Esters form when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid, releasing water.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils reverse the order of the name.

check.q: Which ester is made from propanol and methanoic acid?
check.why: Alcohol part first (propyl), then the acid stem with -oate (methanoate).

practice: Write the formula of ethanoic acid.
Name the ester from ethanol and propanoic acid.
Why is sodium carbonate added at the end of the practical?
independent: Core: Describe the method for making ethyl ethanoate.
Extend: Explain why ethanoic acid is a weak acid. [2 marks]
Stretch: Compare the reaction of ethanoic acid and hydrochloric acid of the same concentration with magnesium. [3 marks]
exit: Define ester. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: name one ester and its use.
lessons.homework: Write an equation for making any ester and name all species.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: flash cards for names (stem + yl/oate). Stretch: why does the reaction use an acid catalyst?

lessons.title: Condensation polymers and biopolyesters
lessons.bigQuestion: How is nylon different from poly(ethene), and why do we want plastics that rot?
objectives: Describe condensation polymerisation for polyamides and polyesters
Compare condensation and addition polymerisation
Describe biopolyesters and the issues with disposal
successCriteria: All: define condensation polymerisation
Most: draw block diagrams of the repeat units
Some: evaluate biopolyesters and recycling
lessons.crossCurricular: Technology: textiles; Environmental science: plastic waste
lessons.smsc: Stewardship: reducing plastic waste and caring for the environment

keywords.def: polymer formed when monomers join and lose a small molecule, such as water
polymer containing amide links, e.g. nylon
polymer containing ester links, e.g. PET
biodegradable polyester made by microorganisms

starter: What is formed when ethene polymerises?
State the functional group in an ester.

teach.heading: Condensation polymerisation
bullets: Two different monomers, each with two functional groups
Monomers join; a small molecule (water) is lost
teach.note: Contrast with addition polymers: only one product and monomers have C=C. Use block diagrams: HO–[ ]–OH (diol) with HOOC–[ ]–COOH (diacid) → …–OOC–[ ]–COO–[ ]–… + H₂O. Nylon: diamine + dicarboxylic acid.

teach.heading: Addition v condensation
bullets: Addition: one monomer type with C=C; only polymer forms
Condensation: two functional groups per monomer; polymer + water
teach.note: PET, from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, is used in drinks bottles and polyester fabric.

teach.heading: Model: block diagram of a polyester
bullets: Join with an ester link, remove H₂O
teach.note: Ask which atoms are lost: the –OH from the acid and the H from the alcohol, together forming water.

model.problem: Show how a polyester forms from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid.
steps: –OH of the acid and H of the alcohol are removed as H₂O
The monomers join by the ester link –COO–
model.answer: Repeat unit with ester link; water released each time

teach.heading: Biopolyesters and disposal
teach.note: Many plastics persist in landfill and oceans. Recycling PET into new bottles or fibres reduces waste; sorting is needed. Biopolyesters (e.g. PHB) break down by microorganisms but may not degrade in all conditions. Proteins are natural polyamides made from amino acids.

misconception.wrong: All condensation polymers are biodegradable.
misconception.right: Nylon and PET resist rotting; only biopolyesters are designed to be broken down by microorganisms.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils say hydrogen or carbon dioxide because water is the usual product of other reactions they know.

check.q: What small molecule is released when nylon forms from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid?
check.why: Each amide link forms with the loss of one water molecule.

practice: State two differences between addition and condensation polymerisation.
Name the link in a polyester.
State one advantage of a biopolyester.
independent: Core: Draw a block diagram for the formation of nylon.
Extend: Explain why PET is called a condensation polymer. [2 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate biopolyesters as a replacement for oil-based plastic bags. [4 marks]
exit: Define condensation polymer. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: nylon versus poly(ethene) and plastics that rot.
lessons.homework: Make a summary diagram of polymers: addition, condensation and biopolymers.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded blocks on cards. Stretch: why does nylon have strong intermolecular forces?
