lessons.title: Stellar evolution compared: Sun-like stars and massive stars
lessons.bigQuestion: Will the Sun end with a bang or a whimper?
objectives: Describe the evolution of Sun-like stars from nebula to white dwarf
Describe the evolution of stars more massive than the Sun
Explain how mass decides a star's final stage
successCriteria: All: order the stages for a Sun-like star
Most: compare the end stages of the two types of star
Some: explain stability on the main sequence and the origin of heavier elements
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: origin of the elements; History: Islamic astronomers' observations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the life and end of stars

keywords.def: a cloud of dust and gas where stars form
long, stable stage where hydrogen fuses to helium in the core
large cool star after the core hydrogen is used up
explosion of a massive star at the end of its life

starter: Bismillah. State what force pulls a nebula together.
State what happens in the core of a main sequence star.

teach.heading: Sun-like stars
bullets: Nebula: a cloud of gas and dust
Protostar forms as gravity pulls the cloud together
Main sequence: hydrogen fuses into helium
teach.note: Sequence: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf. Gravity pulls inwards; heat and radiation pressure from fusion push outwards; main sequence is stable because they balance. When the hydrogen in the core is used up, the core contracts and the outer layers expand and cool (red giant). The outer layers drift off and the core remains as a hot dense white dwarf, which cools over time (approx. billions of years).

teach.heading: Massive stars
bullets: Same start: nebula, protostar, main sequence
Then expand to a red supergiant
Core collapses and a supernova explodes
Leaves a neutron star or black hole
teach.note: The spec points focus on the stages. Very massive stars create heavier elements by fusion, up to iron in the core, and the supernova spreads elements into space, which form new stars, planets and us. A neutron star is extremely dense; if the core is massive enough, a black hole forms (gravity so strong that not even light escapes).

teach.heading: Compare the paths
bullets: The mass of the star decides its fate
Both start with nebula, protostar, main sequence
Larger mass: shorter life on the main sequence
Heavier elements formed and spread in a supernova
teach.note: Ask: why do bigger stars live shorter lives? They use fuel much faster. Model answer below.

model.problem: Describe the differences between the life cycle of the Sun and a star much more massive than the Sun.
steps: Both begin as a nebula that collapses to a protostar and then a main sequence star
The Sun becomes a red giant; the massive star becomes a red supergiant
The Sun's outer layers drift away leaving a white dwarf
The massive star ends in a supernova leaving a neutron star or black hole
model.answer: Mass decides the end stage: white dwarf for Sun-like stars; neutron star or black hole for much more massive stars.

teach.heading: Check: end stages
teach.note: Option A is the typical error of putting a black hole after any star. Option C is the wrong order.

check.q: Which is the final stage of a star like the Sun?
check.why: The Sun is not massive enough to become a supernova. It will end as a white dwarf.

practice: Put in order: red giant, nebula, main sequence, white dwarf, protostar.
State what balances gravity during the main sequence.
State two differences between the end of the Sun and a more massive star.
independent: Core: Draw a flow chart for the life cycle of the Sun.
Extend: Draw a flow chart for a massive star and compare the two.
Stretch: Explain why heavy elements on Earth came from earlier stars.
exit: State the stage after the main sequence for a Sun-like star.
State what may be left after a supernova.
Big question: how does the Sun end?
lessons.homework: Create a labelled life-cycle diagram of the Sun with a one-sentence explanation for each stage.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide stage cards for sorting with pictures. Stretch: explain why stable stars need a balance of forces.

lessons.bigQuestion: If we plot every star by brightness and temperature, what pattern appears?
objectives: Draw the main components of the Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram
Place main sequence stars, red giants and white dwarfs
Use the diagram to follow the life of a star

Most: place the Sun and describe star movements
Some: use the diagram to compare stars' luminosity, temperature and size
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: graphs with reversed axes; Astronomy
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: finding order in what looks random

keywords.def: total energy emitted per second by a star
temperature at a star's visible surface, in kelvin
band of stars in the H-R diagram where stars fuse hydrogen
small, hot, dim star

starter: Bismillah. State what makes a star hot.
Name the final stage of a Sun-like star.
State what colour hot stars appear.

teach.heading: The axes
bullets: Hot blue stars on the left; cool red on the right
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Physics (4PH1) content. The unusual axis, with temperature decreasing from left to right, is a historic convention. Luminosity is often a log scale, with the Sun at 1. Typical temperatures: the Sun's surface is about 5800 K (approx.; verify); hot blue stars exceed 10 000 K. Colour: hot blue-white, then yellow, then orange and red.

teach.heading: Groups of stars
bullets: Main sequence: diagonal band, top left to bottom right
Red giants and supergiants: top right
The Sun is in the middle of the main sequence
teach.note: Draw a sketch on the board. Red giants are cool but very luminous, so they must be very large. White dwarfs are hot but dim, so they must be very small. Most stars (about 90%, approx.) are on the main sequence. Stars move on the diagram as they evolve: from the main sequence to red giant, and then to the white dwarf region.
cycle: Moves up and right as a red giant
Core shrinks and outer layers lost
Ends in the white dwarf region

teach.heading: Draw the diagram
bullets: Mark red giants, supergiants and white dwarfs
teach.note: Pupils sketch their own. Marks usually go for correct axes (with temperature reversed), position of main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.

model.problem: Sketch an H-R diagram and explain the position of white dwarfs.
steps: Vertical axis luminosity, horizontal axis temperature decreasing to the right
Main sequence: band from top left to bottom right
Red giants: top right; white dwarfs: bottom left
White dwarfs are hot but have low luminosity, so they must be very small
model.answer: White dwarfs sit at bottom left: hot but small and dim.

teach.heading: Check: reading the diagram
teach.note: Option B confuses cool with hot. Option D reverses small and large.

check.q: A star is cool but has a high luminosity. Where is it on the H-R diagram?
check.why: Cool stars are on the right; high luminosity means near the top. They are red giants or supergiants and are very large.

lessons.title: Evolution of the universe and the case for the Big Bang
lessons.bigQuestion: What evidence tells us the universe had a beginning?
objectives: Describe the past evolution of the universe according to the Big Bang theory
State the evidence for the Big Bang: red-shift and the cosmic microwave background
Evaluate how well the evidence supports the theory
successCriteria: All: describe the Big Bang in a sentence
Most: explain how red-shift and the CMB support it
Some: evaluate the evidence and compare it with the steady-state theory
lessons.crossCurricular: History of science; Philosophy: evidence and belief
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the universe as a sign; scientific theories change as evidence changes

keywords.def: the universe began from a hot, dense state and has been expanding since
stretching of light from a receding galaxy to longer wavelengths
microwave radiation arriving from all directions in space
the increase in distance between galaxies

starter: State where microwaves come in the electromagnetic spectrum.
State what the Doppler effect is.

teach.heading: The Big Bang model
bullets: The universe began very small, hot and dense
It has expanded and cooled over time
Time began about 13.8 billion years ago (approx.)
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Physics (4PH1) content. Avoid saying it was an explosion into empty space: space itself expands. Ask pupils to draw dots on a balloon, inflate, and watch the dots move apart; there is no centre. The age is approximately 13.8 billion years (verify the value used by the board). Check before use: Time began about 13.8 billion years ago (approx.; verify)

timeline.label: Later
timeline.text: Matter clumps into stars and galaxies

teach.heading: Evidence 1: red-shift
bullets: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted
Galaxies are moving away from us
More distant galaxies show greater red-shift
teach.note: Link to the Doppler effect: waves from a receding source are stretched to longer wavelength. Extrapolating backwards in time, all matter was once together. Pupils must say 'more distant galaxies are moving away faster'. Do not imply that Earth is at the centre.

misconception.wrong: Red-shift shows that the Earth is at the centre of the universe.
misconception.right: Every distant galaxy sees others moving away, like dots on an inflating balloon. There is no centre.

teach.heading: Evidence 2: cosmic microwave background
bullets: Remnant of the hot early universe
Stretched to microwave wavelength by expansion
teach.note: The CMB is radiation released early in the universe's history. As space expanded the wavelength stretched from very short to the microwave region; today it corresponds to about 2.7 K (approx.; verify). The Big Bang predicted it before it was found. Competing steady-state theory could not explain it.

model.problem: Explain how red-shift and the CMB support the Big Bang theory.
steps: Red-shift: galaxies move away from us, so the universe is expanding
More distant galaxies move away faster, matching an expanding universe
Expansion backwards in time suggests a hot dense start
CMB: leftover radiation from the early hot universe, stretched to microwaves, seen from all directions
model.answer: Red-shift shows expansion and the CMB shows a hot early universe, both predicted by the Big Bang theory.

teach.heading: Check: evidence
teach.note: Option A would be blue-shift. Option D is a common wrong claim.

check.q: Light from a distant galaxy has a longer wavelength than expected. This shows the galaxy is...
check.why: Longer wavelength (red-shift) means the source is moving away from the observer.

teach.heading: Evaluating the theory
bullets: Theories change as new data arrives
teach.note: Discuss science as an ongoing process: theory, prediction, observation. Ask: what would make scientists change their minds? Link to respect for evidence and humility about what we do not know.

practice: State the evidence for an expanding universe.
Explain why the CMB is in the microwave region.
State why the Big Bang is not an explosion into empty space.
independent: Core: Make a timeline of the universe from the Big Bang to now.
Extend: Explain how red-shift evidence supports expansion.
Stretch: Evaluate how the CMB supports the Big Bang more strongly than red-shift alone.
exit: Name two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.
State what red-shift shows.
Big question: what tells us the universe had a beginning?
lessons.homework: Write a balanced paragraph: 'the Big Bang theory is well supported by evidence'. Use at least two pieces of evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use the balloon model and a word bank. Stretch: discuss alternative theories and why they fell out of favour.

lessons.title: Revision: living organisms, cells and enzymes; command words
lessons.bigQuestion: What exactly does an examiner want when a question says 'explain'?
objectives: To understand how to answer 4SD0 questions on living organisms, cells and enzymes using the command words correctly
successCriteria: All: recall the eight characteristics of living organisms and cell structures
Most: answer 'describe' and 'explain' questions to the mark scheme
Some: analyse enzyme data and justify conclusions in full
lessons.crossCurricular: English: precise vocabulary and command words
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest self-assessment and responding to feedback

keywords.def: give a short answer with no explanation
say what happens or what something is like
give reasons: say why or how, using 'because'
organism whose cells have a nucleus
enzyme active site changed so substrate no longer fits

hook.text: Two answers to 'Explain why enzymes stop working at 70 °C': 'They die' and 'The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits'. Which gets the marks, and why?
hook.a: The second: it gives the mechanism; enzymes are molecules and are not alive, so they do not die.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'We have certainly created the human being in the best of forms' (at-Tin 95:4). Revising how cells and enzymes work is also a reminder of that design.

starter.q: Name the eight characteristics of living organisms (MRS GREN style).
starter.a: Nutrition, respiration, excretion, response, movement, control of internal conditions, reproduction, growth.

starter.q: Name a prokaryote on the specification.

teach.heading: Command words
bullets: Evaluate: both sides and a judgement
teach.note: Show how each command word changes the answer.

head: Command word
What to do
Typical marks
rows: what happens or a pattern with data

teach.heading: Key content
teach.note: Quick-fire recap with the knowledge organiser.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Describe the trend, then explain it
teach.note: Model a 4-mark answer.

model.problem: Describe and explain the effect of temperature on amylase activity. [4 marks]
steps: Describe: activity increases to an optimum of about 40 °C, then falls
Explain rise: more kinetic energy, more successful collisions
Explain fall: active site changes shape, enzyme denatured
Substrate no longer fits, so rate falls to zero
model.answer: One descriptive point and three explanatory points

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which is a feature of ALL viruses?
check.why: Viruses are particles with a protein coat around genetic material; they are not cells.

practice.q: State two features of bacterial cells. [2 marks]
practice.a: Any two: no nucleus; circular chromosomal DNA; plasmids; cell wall; cell membrane; cytoplasm; ribosomes.
practice.model:
'State' means short facts, one mark each.
Fact 1: no nucleus.
Fact 2: plasmids present.
No explanation needed.

practice.q: Explain why pepsin works in the stomach but amylase does not. [2 marks]
practice.a: The stomach is acidic (about pH 2) (1); pepsin's optimum is acidic, while amylase's active site is denatured at low pH (1).

practice.q: Give two differences between plant and fungal cells. [2 marks]
practice.a: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose (1); fungi have no chloroplasts (1).

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Compare the structure of a palisade cell, a yeast cell and a bacterial cell. Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Marks for: all have membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes (1); palisade and yeast have nuclei and mitochondria (1); palisade has chloroplasts, cellulose wall, large vacuole (1); yeast has a wall (chitin) and no chloroplasts (1); bacterium has no nucleus, circular DNA (1) and plasmids, no mitochondria (1).
independent.model: Teacher plans it first as a three-column table, then turns each row into a comparison sentence: 'All three have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes, but only the bacterium lacks a nucleus...'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Starch and amylase at 37 °C: the iodine colour stays blue-black for 20 minutes when the solution is boiled first. Explain.
independent.a: Boiling denatured the amylase (1); active site changed shape (1); starch not digested so iodine stays blue-black (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain why viruses are not classed as living organisms.
independent.a: They show none of the characteristics on their own (1); they can only reproduce inside host cells (1).

exit.q: 'Explain' means...
Big question: what does an examiner want when a question says 'explain'?
exit.a: Reasons using correct science (how or why), linked with 'because' or 'so'.

lessons.title: Revision: movement of substances and transport in plants and humans
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a whale need a heart but an amoeba does not?
objectives: To understand how diffusion, osmosis and transport systems move substances in organisms, and how to answer exam questions on them
successCriteria: All: define diffusion, osmosis and active transport
Most: describe xylem, phloem, blood and the heart
Some: explain why multicellular organisms need transport systems using surface area to volume ratio
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: surface area to volume ratio calculations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the heart, physically and spiritually

keywords.def: surface area divided by volume; smaller in bigger organisms
carries water and mineral ions from the roots
carries sucrose and amino acids
protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen
white blood cell that ingests pathogens

hook.text: An amoeba takes in oxygen through its surface. Why can't a whale do the same?
hook.a: Its surface area to volume ratio is far too small and distances too great, so it needs lungs, blood and a heart.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'In the body there is a piece of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound... it is the heart' (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). The physical heart is the centre of the transport system.

starter.q: Which process needs energy from respiration?
Which vessel carries blood away from the heart?

teach.heading: SA:V ratio
bullets: Small organisms: large SA:V, diffusion enough
Large organisms: small SA:V, need transport systems
teach.note: Model the cube calculation.

teach.heading: Blood and the heart
bullets: Red cells: haemoglobin, no nucleus, biconcave
Plasma carries CO₂, urea, glucose, hormones, heat
teach.note: Heart: right side to lungs, left side to body; adrenaline raises heart rate.

teach.heading: Model answer
teach.note: Model a 3-mark answer.

model.problem: Explain how red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen. [3 marks]
steps: No nucleus: more room for haemoglobin
Biconcave shape: large surface area for diffusion
model.answer: Each feature linked to its function

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: A 3 cm cube has SA:V of...
check.why: SA = 54 cm², V = 27 cm³, ratio 2:1.

practice.q: Describe the role of the xylem and phloem. [2 marks]
practice.a: Xylem carries water and mineral ions from roots to the rest of the plant (1); phloem carries sucrose and amino acids between leaves and other parts (1).
practice.model:
Two tissues, one mark each.
Xylem: what (water and mineral ions) and where (from roots upwards).
Phloem: what (sucrose and amino acids) and where (leaves to other parts).

practice.q: State the function of lymphocytes. [1 mark]
practice.a: Produce antibodies.

practice.q: Explain why arteries have thick, elastic walls. [2 marks]
practice.a: Blood leaves the heart at high pressure (1); thick elastic walls withstand and even out the pressure (1).

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe the path of blood from the vena cava to the aorta, naming chambers, valves and vessels. Portal response box.
independent.a: Vena cava, right atrium (1), valve, right ventricle (1), pulmonary artery to lungs (1), pulmonary vein (1), left atrium, valve, left ventricle (1), aorta (1).
independent.model: Teacher writes the first two marking points: 'Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the vena cava, then passes through a valve into the right ventricle.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 4 marks): Potato cylinders: in water +10%, in 0.5 M sucrose -8%. Explain both results.
independent.a: Water: higher water concentration outside (1), water enters by osmosis (1); 0.5 M: lower water concentration outside (1), water leaves by osmosis (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain how heart rate changes during exercise and why.
independent.a: Heart rate increases (1); muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose (1) and CO₂ must be removed faster (1). Adrenaline also raises heart rate.

exit.q: Large organisms need transport systems because their SA:V is...
Big question: why does a whale need a heart but an amoeba does not?
exit.a: The whale's small SA:V and long distances mean diffusion alone is too slow, so it needs a pumped transport system.

lessons.homework: Complete the transport retrieval quiz on the portal; correct answers in green.
lessons.send: SEND: heart diagram with the route numbered. EAL: atrium, ventricle, xylem, phloem. Stretch: compare transport in plants and humans in a table.

lessons.title: Revision: Chemistry 1 principles: states, separation, atoms and bonding
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does diamond not conduct electricity but graphite does?
objectives: To understand how particle and bonding ideas explain properties, and how to answer Chemistry 1 exam questions
successCriteria: All: recall atomic structure and electronic configurations
Most: choose the right separation method and calculate Rf values
Some: explain properties of ionic, simple molecular and giant covalent substances
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: particle model and states of matter
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: precise measure in all things (al-Qamar 54:49)

keywords.def: distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent
arrangement of electrons in shells, e.g. 2.8.1
weak forces between molecules
lattice of atoms all joined by covalent bonds
electrons free to move through a structure

hook.text: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. One is the hardest natural substance, the other is used in pencils. How?
hook.a: Different structures: diamond has four bonds per atom in 3D; graphite has layers with delocalised electrons.

starter.q: Separation method for salt from salt solution?
Isotopes differ in the number of...

teach.heading: Separation
bullets: Distillation: liquid from solution; fractional for mixtures of liquids
teach.note: Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent front distance.

teach.heading: Structure and properties
bullets: Ionic: high mp, conduct molten or dissolved
Simple molecular: low mp, do not conduct
Giant covalent: very high mp; graphite conducts
teach.note: Use the compare block.

left.title: Diamond
points: no delocalised electrons: does not conduct

right.title: Graphite
points: each C bonded to 3 others in layers

teach.heading: Model answer
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Explain why methane has a low boiling point. [2 marks]
steps: Methane is a simple molecular substance
Little energy needed to overcome them (not the covalent bonds)
model.answer: Weak intermolecular forces need little energy to overcome

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: A spot moves 3.6 cm; solvent front 9.0 cm. Rf?

practice.q: Explain why sodium chloride conducts when molten but not when solid. [2 marks]
practice.a: Solid: ions fixed in the lattice (1); molten: ions free to move and carry charge (1).
practice.model:
Solid state: where are the ions?
Fixed in the lattice, so they cannot move.
Molten: ions free to move, so they carry charge through the liquid.

practice.q: A pure substance melts at a sharp temperature. What does a mixture do? [1 mark]
practice.a: Melts over a range of temperatures.

practice.q: Draw (describe) the dot-and-cross diagram for HCl. [2 marks]
practice.a: One shared pair between H and Cl (1); Cl has three non-bonding pairs, outer shells shown (1).

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 5 marks): A chromatogram of a food colouring shows three spots; one matches E133 (Rf 0.62). Describe how to carry out the experiment and how to identify E133.
independent.a: Pencil start line (1); spots above solvent level (1); lid on, solvent rises (1); measure spot and front distances, Rf = spot ÷ front (1); matching Rf (and position) to a known sample identifies E133 (1).
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first two points: 'Draw a pencil line 1 cm from the bottom (pencil does not dissolve).
Spot the colouring on the line and stand the paper in solvent below the line.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why graphite is used for electrodes and as a lubricant.
independent.a: Delocalised electrons carry charge (1); layers held by weak forces (1) slide over each other (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain why the boiling points of simple molecules increase with relative molecular mass.
independent.a: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces (1), so more energy is needed to separate them (1).

exit.q: Which conducts electricity as a solid?
Big question: why does diamond not conduct but graphite does?
exit.a: Graphite has delocalised electrons between layers; in diamond all outer electrons are in bonds.

lessons.homework: Complete the Chemistry 1 structure and bonding quiz on the portal.
lessons.send: SEND: structure-property table to complete. EAL: lattice, intermolecular, delocalised. Stretch: explain C60 fullerene's properties.

lessons.title: Revision: Physics 1 motion: graphs and equations
lessons.bigQuestion: How much can one graph tell you about a journey?
objectives: To understand how to interpret motion graphs and use the motion equations in exam questions
successCriteria: All: calculate speed and acceleration with units
Most: find acceleration and distance from velocity-time graphs
Some: use v² = u² + 2as and choose the right equation
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: gradients and areas under graphs
lessons.smsc: Moral: safe speeds on roads

keywords.def: distance ÷ time
change in velocity ÷ time
steepness of a graph
distance on a velocity-time graph
speed in a given direction

hook.text: A distance-time graph and a velocity-time graph both have a flat line. Do they mean the same thing?
hook.a: No: flat on distance-time means stationary; flat on velocity-time means constant velocity.

starter.q: Gradient of a distance-time graph gives...

teach.heading: Which equation?
teach.note: Choose by what is given and what is asked.

teach.heading: Reading v-t graphs
teach.note: Model on a three-stage journey.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Write the equation, substitute, answer with unit
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: A cyclist at 5 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² over 24 m. Find the final velocity. [3 marks]

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Total distance for the three-stage journey?

practice.q: A car goes from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. Acceleration? [2 marks]
practice.model:
Formula: a = (v - u) ÷ t.
Substitute: (10 - 30) ÷ 4 = -20 ÷ 4.
Answer: -5 m/s² (a deceleration of 5 m/s²).

practice.q: Describe how to find speed from a curved distance-time graph at a given time. [2 marks]
practice.a: Draw a tangent (1); find its gradient (1).

practice.q: A ball dropped from rest falls 45 m (a = 10 m/s²). Speed on landing?

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): A train's v-t graph: 0 to 20 m/s in 40 s, constant for 60 s, stops in 20 s. Calculate the acceleration in each stage and the total distance.
independent.model: Teacher works stage 1: a = 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5 m/s²; distance = ½ × 40 × 20 = 400 m.

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 2 marks): Calculate the average speed of the train for the whole journey.
Stretch (exam-style, 3 marks): Describe a practical to investigate the motion of a toy car down a ramp (4SD0 1.5).
independent.a: Mark distances on the ramp (1); time with a stopwatch or light gates at each mark (1); calculate speed = distance ÷ time; repeat and average (1).

exit.q: The area under a velocity-time graph is the...
Big question: how much can one graph tell you about a journey?
exit.a: A velocity-time graph gives acceleration (gradient), distance (area) and when the object is speeding up, steady or slowing.

lessons.title: Revision: Physics 1 forces: F = ma, weight, stopping and springs
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do motorway speed limits matter so much in the rain?
objectives: To understand how forces affect motion and how to answer exam questions on F = ma, stopping distance and Hooke's law
successCriteria: All: calculate resultant force, F = ma and W = mg
Most: explain factors affecting thinking and braking distance
Some: describe the spring practical and interpret force-extension graphs
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: road safety
lessons.smsc: Moral: driving and cycling safely to protect others

keywords.def: single force with the same effect as all the forces
distance travelled during reaction time
distance travelled while braking
extension is proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality
constant velocity when resultant force is zero

hook.text: Rain doubles braking distance but not thinking distance. Why only one?
hook.a: Wet roads reduce friction between tyres and road; thinking distance depends on reaction time and speed.

starter.q: Is force a scalar or a vector?

teach.heading: Forces and motion
bullets: Resultant zero: constant velocity or at rest
teach.note: Terminal velocity: weight equals drag.

teach.heading: Stopping distance
bullets: Thinking: speed, reaction time (tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distraction)
Braking: speed, mass, road and tyre condition, brakes
teach.note: Data from a typical stopping chart.

teach.heading: Springs
bullets: Straight line through origin: Hooke's law
Beyond the limit: curve; may not return
teach.note: Model the graph reading.

model.problem: A spring extends 4 cm with 2 N. Assuming Hooke's law, what is the extension with 5 N? [2 marks]
model.answer: 10 cm (if within the limit of proportionality)

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which increases thinking distance?
check.why: Tiredness increases reaction time; the others affect braking distance.

practice.q: A 1500 kg car: driving force 4000 N, resistive force 1000 N. Acceleration? [3 marks]
practice.model: Step 1: resultant = 4000 - 1000 = 3000 N. Step 2: a = F ÷ m = 3000 ÷ 1500. Step 3: a = 2 m/s².

practice.q: Weight of a 75 kg astronaut on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg)?
Give two factors that increase braking distance. [2 marks]
practice.a: Any two: higher speed, greater mass, wet or icy road, worn tyres, worn brakes.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe how to investigate the extension of a spring with force, including how to make results accurate. Portal response box.
independent.a: Clamp spring and ruler (1); measure original length (1); add masses 100 g at a time, W = mg (1); measure new length at eye level, calculate extension (1); repeat and average (1); plot force against extension (1).
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first two points: 'Hang the spring from a clamp next to a vertical ruler.
Record its original length with a pointer, reading at eye level.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why a skydiver reaches terminal velocity.
independent.a: Weight constant; air resistance increases with speed (1); eventually equals weight (1); resultant force zero so velocity constant (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain what is meant by elastic behaviour.
independent.a: The material returns to its original shape (1) when the force is removed (1).

exit.q: Hooke's law: extension is proportional to...
Big question: why do speed limits matter so much in the rain?
exit.a: Wet roads reduce friction, so braking distance increases; at higher speed both thinking and braking distance rise.

lessons.send: SEND: formula sheet; graph-reading prompts. EAL: resultant, braking, extension. Stretch: explain why braking distance increases with the square of speed.

lessons.title: Revision: photosynthesis and human nutrition
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does the energy in your breakfast originally come from?
objectives: To understand photosynthesis, limiting factors and human nutrition well enough to answer 4SD0 exam questions
successCriteria: All: write the word and balanced equations for photosynthesis
Most: explain limiting factors and the starch test
Some: link digestion, enzymes and absorption in extended answers
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: endothermic reactions and balanced equations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah sends down rain and brings out plants (al-An'am 6:99)

keywords.def: plants make glucose from CO₂ and water using light
the factor in shortest supply that limits the rate
green pigment that absorbs light
break fats into small droplets
projections that increase surface area for absorption

hook.text: Every meal you eat can be traced back to a plant capturing sunlight. Can you think of one that cannot?
hook.a: Almost none: even meat and milk come from animals that ate plants; salt and water are exceptions.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'It is He who sends down rain from the sky, and We produce thereby the growth of all things, and We produce from it greenery' (al-An'am 6:99). Photosynthesis is how that greenery turns light into food.

starter.q: Name the enzyme that digests lipids.

teach.heading: Photosynthesis
teach.note: Use the limiting factor graph.

teach.heading: Human nutrition
teach.note: Quick recall grid.

teach.heading: Model answer
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Explain the shape of the graph above 6 units of light. [2 marks]
steps: Light is no longer the limiting factor
Another factor, such as CO₂ concentration or temperature, now limits the rate

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: In the starch test on a leaf, why is the leaf boiled in ethanol?
check.why: Removing the green chlorophyll lets the iodine colour be seen.

practice.q: Describe how to test a leaf for starch. [4 marks]
practice.a: Boil in water to kill and soften (1); in ethanol (in a hot water bath, no flame) to remove chlorophyll (1); rinse in water (1); add iodine: blue-black shows starch (1).
practice.model: Four steps, four marks: boil in water, warm in ethanol in a water bath, rinse, add iodine and look for blue-black.

practice.q: State the function of fibre in the diet. [1 mark]
practice.a: Helps food move through the gut by peristalsis (prevents constipation).

practice.q: Explain why bile helps lipase. [2 marks]
practice.a: Bile emulsifies fat into small droplets (1), giving a larger surface area for lipase (1).

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Explain how a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. Portal response box.
independent.a: Large surface area (1); thin, short diffusion distance (1); many chloroplasts in palisade layer near the top (1); stomata let CO₂ in (1); air spaces in spongy layer (1); veins (xylem) bring water (1).
independent.model: Teacher plans with a feature-reason table: 'Broad and flat: large surface area to absorb light.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): A variegated leaf (green and white) is tested for starch. Only the green parts turn blue-black. Explain.
independent.a: Only green parts have chlorophyll (1); chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis (1); so only they made glucose stored as starch (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain why a pregnant woman needs more iron and calcium.
independent.a: Iron for extra haemoglobin for her and the fetus (1); calcium for the fetus's bones and teeth (1).

exit.q: The factor in shortest supply is the...
Big question: where does the energy in your breakfast originally come from?
exit.a: Light from the Sun, captured by plants in photosynthesis.

lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding harm to the body (al-Baqarah 2:195)

keywords.def: releases energy from glucose using oxygen
releases energy without oxygen
movement of air into and out of the lungs
air sacs adapted for gas exchange
molecule that provides energy for cells

hook.text: A student writes: 'Plants photosynthesise during the day and respire at night.' What is wrong?
hook.a: Plants respire all the time, day and night; they also photosynthesise when there is light.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction' (al-Baqarah 2:195). Knowing how smoking damages the gas exchange system helps us protect the trust of our bodies.

starter.q: Products of anaerobic respiration in muscles?
Name the muscles between the ribs.
Gas that binds haemoglobin from smoke?

teach.heading: Respiration
bullets: Plants and yeast anaerobic: glucose → ethanol + CO₂
teach.note: Aerobic releases much more energy (more ATP).

teach.heading: Gas exchange
bullets: Alveoli: large SA, thin walls, capillaries, moist
teach.note: Quick recall.

teach.heading: Model answer
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Explain why boiled seeds are used in the respiring seeds experiment. [2 marks]
steps: Boiled seeds are dead and do not respire
They act as a control to show any temperature rise is due to respiration
model.answer: Control; dead seeds do not respire

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Breathing in: thorax volume and pressure...
check.why: Volume increases so pressure falls below atmospheric; air flows in.

practice.q: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration. [2 marks]
practice.a: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
practice.model:
Correct formulae for glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water (1).
Balance carbon (6CO₂), hydrogen (6H₂O), then oxygen (6O₂) (1).

practice.q: State two adaptations of alveoli. [2 marks]
practice.a: Large surface area; walls one cell thick (or good blood supply; moist).

practice.q: Explain how tar damages the airways. [2 marks]
practice.a: Tar damages cilia (1) so mucus is not cleared, causing infections and bronchitis (1). (Tar also contains carcinogens.)

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe how breathing in and out happens. Portal response box.
independent.a: In: intercostals contract, ribs up and out (1); diaphragm contracts and flattens (1); volume increases, pressure falls, air in (1). Out: intercostals relax, ribs down and in (1); diaphragm relaxes and domes (1); volume decreases, pressure rises, air out (1).
independent.model: Teacher writes breathing in as three linked points, then pupils write breathing out in the same structure.

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 4 marks): Describe an experiment to show that exhaled air contains more CO₂ than inhaled air.
independent.a: Two tubes of limewater (or hydrogencarbonate indicator) (1); breathe in through one, out through the other (1); exhaled tube turns milky (or yellow) faster (1); same volume and time (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why a sprinter keeps breathing deeply after a race.
independent.a: Anaerobic respiration made lactic acid (1); oxygen is needed to break it down (oxygen debt) (1); so breathing rate and depth stay high (1).

exit.q: Yeast anaerobic respiration produces...
Big question: how are breathing, gas exchange and respiration linked and different?
exit.a: Breathing moves air; gas exchange moves O₂ into and CO₂ out of blood at the alveoli; respiration is the reaction in cells that uses O₂ and makes CO₂.

keywords.def: metals listed from most to least reactive
a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one
gain of oxygen or loss of electrons
loss of oxygen or gain of electrons
a more reactive metal corrodes instead of iron

hook.text: Zinc blocks are fixed to steel ship hulls and slowly disappear. Why would anyone want that?
hook.a: Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron: sacrificial protection.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for people' (al-Hadid 57:25). Knowing why iron rusts and how to protect it is part of using that benefit wisely.

starter.q: Percentage of oxygen in dry air?
Colour of bromine at room temperature?
Gas made when a metal reacts with dilute acid?

teach.heading: Group trends
bullets: Group 1: reactivity increases down the group
Group 7: reactivity decreases down the group
Group 7: colours darken, melting points rise
teach.note: Predict for unfamiliar elements.

right.title: Group 7
points: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one
darker and higher mp down the group

teach.heading: Reactivity series
bullets: K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au
Order from reactions with water, acid and displacement
teach.note: Displacement grid example.

teach.heading: Model answer
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu. Identify what is oxidised and reduced. [2 marks]
steps: Mg loses electrons to form Mg²⁺: oxidised
Cu²⁺ gains electrons to form Cu: reduced

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution. What forms?
check.why: Chlorine is more reactive and displaces iodine: solution turns brown.

practice.q: Predict how rubidium reacts with water. [2 marks]
practice.a: Very vigorously, more than potassium (1); forms rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen (1).
practice.model:
Trend: reactivity increases down Group 1.
Rubidium is below potassium, so it reacts even more violently.
Products: metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

practice.q: Use the grid to put Mg, Zn and Cu in order of reactivity.
practice.a: Mg > Zn > Cu

practice.q: Explain how galvanising protects iron. [2 marks]
practice.a: Zinc coating is a barrier to air and water (1); zinc is more reactive so corrodes first even if scratched (1).

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe how to find the percentage of oxygen in air using iron wool (or copper and syringes), and explain the result. Portal response box.
independent.a: Known volume of air (1); iron wool in a measuring cylinder over water (1); leave several days (1); iron rusts, using oxygen (1); water rises; measure volume change (1); about 21% (1).
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first two points: 'Push damp iron wool to the bottom of a measuring cylinder and invert it in water.
Record the starting volume of air.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why aluminium does not seem as reactive as its position suggests.
independent.a: Aluminium has a protective oxide layer (1) that stops air and water reaching the metal (1), so it reacts slowly (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Write a balanced equation for sodium reacting with water.
independent.a: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

exit.q: Most reactive of these?
Big question: why is potassium stored under oil but gold found as metal?
exit.a: Potassium is very reactive and would react with air and water; gold is unreactive so it stays uncombined.

keywords.def: compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal
insoluble solid formed in a solution
test that identifies metal ions by flame colour
an acid in terms of proton transfer
acid + base → salt + water

hook.text: A white powder gives a lilac flame and a white precipitate with acidified barium chloride. What is it?
hook.a: Potassium sulfate.

starter.q: Acids produce which ions in water?

teach.heading: Tests for ions
bullets: Flame tests: Li⁺ red, Na⁺ yellow, K⁺ lilac, Ca²⁺ orange-red, Cu²⁺ blue-green
NaOH: Cu²⁺ blue, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ brown precipitates
NH₄⁺: warm with NaOH, gas turns damp red litmus blue
teach.note: Learn as a table.

teach.heading: Tests for gases
bullets: H₂: squeaky pop; O₂: relights glowing splint
CO₂: limewater milky; NH₃: damp red litmus blue
teach.note: Water: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate white to blue; pure water boils at 100 °C.

teach.heading: Making copper sulfate
bullets: Warm acid, add excess copper(II) oxide
Heat to concentrate, leave to crystallise; dry
teach.note: Model the 6-mark method.

model.problem: Describe how to make pure, dry copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide. [6 marks]
steps: Warm dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker
Add copper(II) oxide until in excess (no more dissolves)
Heat the filtrate to evaporate some water
Pat crystals dry on filter paper

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: A solution gives a green precipitate with NaOH. It contains...
check.why: Iron(II) hydroxide is green; iron(III) is brown; copper(II) is blue.

practice.q: Why is the copper(II) oxide added in excess? [1 mark]
practice.a: To make sure all the acid has reacted.
practice.model:
If oxide is left over, all the acid has been used up.
So the salt solution has no acid left in it.

practice.q: A substance gives a yellow flame and a cream precipitate with silver nitrate. Name it. [2 marks]
practice.a: Sodium (1) bromide (1).

practice.q: Universal indicator turns purple. pH and type?
practice.a: About 13 to 14: strong alkali.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Three unlabelled solutions: sodium chloride, iron(III) sulfate, ammonium carbonate. Describe tests to identify each, with results. Portal response box.
independent.a: Flame test: Na⁺ yellow (1); AgNO₃ with HNO₃: white precipitate for Cl⁻ (1); NaOH: brown precipitate for Fe³⁺ (1); BaCl₂ with HCl: white precipitate for sulfate (1); warm with NaOH: ammonia turns damp red litmus blue (1); acid: CO₂ turns limewater milky for carbonate (1).
independent.model:
Teacher does sodium chloride first: 'Flame test: yellow flame shows Na⁺.
Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate: white precipitate shows Cl⁻.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain, in terms of protons, why ammonia acts as a base.
independent.a: A base is a proton acceptor (1); ammonia accepts H⁺ to form NH₄⁺ (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Write a balanced equation for copper(II) oxide reacting with sulfuric acid.
independent.a: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O

exit.q: Test for chloride ions?
exit.a: Nitric acid then silver nitrate: white precipitate
options: Nitric acid then silver nitrate: white precipitate

exit.q: Big question: how can you prove what is in an unlabelled powder?
exit.a: Dissolve it and do flame and precipitate tests for the cation and anion, comparing with known results.

keywords.def: thin wire that melts when current is too high
safety wire connecting a metal case to earth
current that changes direction (mains)
energy per second, P = IV
energy per unit charge

hook.text: A metal toaster has a loose live wire touching its case. Why does the earth wire stop you getting a shock?
hook.a: Current flows down the low-resistance earth wire; the large current melts the fuse and cuts off the supply.

starter.q: Mains in the UK is a.c. or d.c.?

teach.heading: Equations
bullets: V = IR; P = IV; E = IVt
teach.note: Equation sheet check.

teach.heading: Safety
bullets: Fuse in the live wire melts if current too high
Double insulation: plastic cases, no earth needed
teach.note: Choose fuse just above the normal current.

teach.heading: Model answer
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: A 2.3 kW kettle on 230 V. Which fuse: 3 A, 5 A or 13 A? [3 marks]
steps: Choose the next fuse above: 13 A

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: A 1.2 kW hairdryer on 230 V. Best fuse?
check.why: I = 1200 ÷ 230 = 5.2 A, so 5 A would melt; choose 13 A.

practice.q: A heater draws 8 A from 230 V for 30 minutes. Energy transferred? [3 marks]
Explain why the fuse is in the live wire. [2 marks]
practice.a: So when it melts the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage (1); the appliance is safe to touch (1).

practice.q: A 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistor in series on 9 V. Current?

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Explain how the earth wire and fuse work together to protect a person using a metal kettle with a fault. Portal response box.
independent.a: Live wire touches the metal case (1); earth wire connects case to ground with low resistance (1); large current flows to earth (1); current exceeds fuse rating (1); fuse melts, breaking the live connection (1); case is no longer live, so no shock (1).
independent.model: Teacher writes the first link: 'If a fault makes the live wire touch the metal case, a large current flows through the low-resistance earth wire rather than through a person.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): In parallel: lamp A (12 Ω) and lamp B (6 Ω) on 6 V. Find each current and the supply current.
Stretch (exam-style, 3 marks): 120 C of charge passes through a lamp in 1 minute, transferring 720 J. Find current and voltage.

exit.q: The earth wire is connected to the...
Big question: why does a kettle need a 13 A fuse but a lamp only 3 A?
exit.a: The kettle has a much higher power, so it draws a larger current (about 10 A); the lamp draws well under 3 A.

lessons.title: Revision: coordination: nerves, the eye and plant responses

keywords.def: a change in the environment
detects a stimulus
a muscle or gland that responds
gap between neurones crossed by neurotransmitters
plant hormone that causes cell elongation

hook.text: Plants have no nerves, yet a seedling on a windowsill bends towards the light. How?
hook.a: Auxin collects on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate, so the stem bends towards the light.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And Allah brought you out of your mothers' wombs knowing nothing, and gave you hearing and sight and hearts, that perhaps you would be grateful' (an-Nahl 16:78).

starter.q: Part of the eye that detects light?
Roots grow towards gravity. Name the response.

teach.heading: Reflex arc
teach.note: Use the cycle.

bullets: Near object: ciliary muscles contract, ligaments slacken, lens fatter
Far object: ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tighten, lens thinner
Bright light: circular iris muscles contract, pupil smaller
teach.note: Compare near and far.

teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Explain why a shoot bends towards light from one side. [3 marks]
steps: Auxin moves to the shaded side
Auxin causes cells there to elongate more
Shaded side grows faster, so the shoot bends towards light

check.q: In a reflex arc, the relay neurone is in the...

practice.q: Describe the pathway of a reflex arc when touching a hot object. [4 marks]
practice.a: Receptor in skin detects heat (1); impulse along sensory neurone (1); relay neurone in spinal cord, synapses (1); motor neurone to muscle (effector) which contracts (1).
practice.model:
Follow the cycle: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
One mark per correct linked step.

practice.q: How is the impulse passed across a synapse? [2 marks]
practice.a: Neurotransmitter is released (1) and diffuses across the gap to the next neurone (1).

practice.q: Compare nervous and hormonal responses. [2 marks]
practice.a: Nervous: electrical, fast, short-lived (1); hormonal: chemical in blood, slower, longer-lasting (1).

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Explain how the eye changes to focus on a book after looking out of a window. Portal response box.
independent.a: Light from near object diverges more (1); ciliary muscles contract (1); suspensory ligaments slacken (1); lens becomes fatter/more rounded (1); refracts light more (1); image focused on retina (1).
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first two points: 'The book is near, so the lens must refract light more.
The ciliary muscles contract...'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Describe how to investigate the effect of light from one side on seedlings.
independent.a: Grow seedlings in two boxes, one with a slit on one side (1); same type, number, water, temperature (1); after several days observe direction of growth (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain why reflexes are important for survival.
independent.a: They are fast and automatic (1), protecting the body from harm before conscious thought (1).

exit.q: In bright light the pupil...
Big question: how does your hand move before you feel pain?
exit.a: A reflex arc through the spinal cord sends an impulse to the muscle before the brain processes the pain.

lessons.bigQuestion: How does your body keep its temperature near 37 °C in both summer and winter?
objectives: To understand homeostasis, temperature control, hormones and excretion well enough to write precise exam answers

Most: explain temperature control by sweating, vasodilation and vasoconstriction

lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the balance Allah placed within the body

keywords.def: keeping internal conditions constant
widening of blood vessels near the skin
narrowing of blood vessels near the skin
chemical messenger carried in the blood
removal of waste products of metabolism

hook.text: A common mistake is 'blood vessels move closer to the skin when hot'. What really happens?
hook.a: Arterioles supplying skin capillaries widen (vasodilation); vessels do not move.

teach.heading: Temperature control
teach.note: Skin's role.

teach.heading: Hormones (4SD0 list)
teach.note: Learn the table.

head: Hormone
Gland
Effect
rows: raises heart rate, prepares for action

teach.heading: Model answer
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Explain how vasodilation helps cool the body. [3 marks]
steps: Arterioles near the skin surface widen
More blood flows through skin capillaries
More heat is lost from the skin by radiation
model.answer: Widened vessels carry more blood to the surface to lose heat

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Sweating cools the body because...
options: evaporation of sweat transfers heat from the skin
check.why: Water evaporating from the skin takes thermal energy with it.

practice.q: Define homeostasis. [1 mark]
practice.a: Maintaining a constant internal environment.
practice.model: One clear sentence with the key idea: keeping internal conditions (such as temperature and water content) constant.

practice.q: Name two excretory products of the skin. [2 marks]
practice.a: Water and urea (and salts) in sweat.

practice.q: Explain why shivering warms the body. [2 marks]
practice.a: Muscles contract rapidly (1), respiration increases releasing heat (1).

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe how the body responds when its temperature rises above 37 °C. Portal response box.
independent.a: Change detected by receptors/brain (1); sweat glands produce more sweat (1); evaporation transfers heat (1); arterioles to skin dilate (1); more blood near surface (1); more heat lost by radiation (1).
independent.model:
Teacher starts: 'The rise in temperature is detected by the brain.
Sweat glands in the skin release more sweat...'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 2 marks): Compare the speed and duration of nervous and hormonal responses using adrenaline as an example.
independent.a: Nervous responses are faster but short-lived (1); adrenaline travels in the blood, acts more slowly but lasts longer (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 3 marks): After a meal, blood glucose rises. Describe the role of insulin.
independent.a: Pancreas detects the rise (1) and releases insulin into the blood (1); insulin causes glucose to be taken up by cells and stored (as glycogen in the liver), lowering blood glucose (1).

exit.q: When cold, blood vessels to the skin...
Big question: how does your body keep its temperature near 37 °C?
exit.a: Sweating and vasodilation lose heat when hot; vasoconstriction and shivering keep heat when cold.

check.why: Mr of CH₂O = 30; 180 ÷ 30 = 6; C₆H₁₂O₆.

practice.q: Theoretical yield of NaCl was 11.7 g; actual 9.36 g. % yield? [2 marks]
practice.model: % yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100 = 9.36 ÷ 11.7 × 100 = 80%.

practice.q: Calculate Mr of Mg(OH)₂ (Mg 24, O 16, H 1).
Find the empirical formula of a compound with 2.8 g Fe and 1.2 g O (Fe 56).
practice.a: Fe 0.05, O 0.075; ratio 2:3; Fe₂O₃

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. (a) Calculate the mass of CaO from 25 g CaCO₃. (b) 11.2 g is collected; calculate % yield. (c) Give two reasons it is below 100%.
independent.a: (a) 0.25 mol × 56 = 14 g (3 marks); (b) 11.2 ÷ 14 × 100 = 80% (1); (c) incomplete decomposition; loss in transfer (2).
independent.model: Teacher works (a): moles CaCO₃ = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25; ratio 1:1; mass CaO = 0.25 × 56 = 14 g.

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): In the metal oxide practical 1.20 g Mg gave 2.00 g oxide. Find the empirical formula.
Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Boron is 20% ¹⁰B and 80% ¹¹B. Calculate Ar.

exit.q: Moles = mass ÷ ...
Big question: how do chemists know how much of each reactant to buy?
exit.a: They convert masses to moles, use the equation's ratio, and convert back to mass, allowing for yield.

lessons.title: Revision: Physics 3 waves and the electromagnetic spectrum
lessons.bigQuestion: What do radio, light and X-rays have in common, and how are they different?
objectives: To understand wave properties, v = fλ and the electromagnetic spectrum well enough to answer 4SD0 exam questions
successCriteria: All: define amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period
Most: use v = fλ and f = 1/T
Some: explain uses and hazards across the EM spectrum
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: UV and skin, the eye detecting visible light
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting ourselves from harmful radiation

keywords.def: oscillations at right angles to the direction of travel
oscillations parallel to the direction of travel
waves per second, in hertz
distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next
family of transverse waves all travelling at the speed of light in a vacuum

hook.text: Waves carry energy across the ocean, but a floating bottle just bobs up and down. What does that tell us?
hook.a: Waves transfer energy, not matter.

starter.q: Which EM wave has the longest wavelength?
Speed of light in a vacuum?

teach.heading: Wave terms
bullets: Waves transfer energy and information, not matter
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: A sound of 500 Hz has a wavelength of 0.68 m. Find its speed. [2 marks]

teach.heading: EM spectrum
bullets: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, UV, X-rays, gamma
Frequency increases from radio to gamma
All travel at the same speed in a vacuum
teach.note: Order and uses.

teach.heading: Doppler effect
bullets: Source moving towards you: higher frequency, shorter wavelength
Moving away: lower frequency, longer wavelength
teach.note: A passing ambulance siren sounds higher then lower.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: A radio wave has f = 100 MHz. Wavelength? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)

practice.q: A wave has period 0.02 s. Frequency? [1 mark]
Give one difference between transverse and longitudinal waves. [1 mark]
practice.a: Transverse oscillations are at right angles to energy transfer; longitudinal are parallel.

practice.q: State one use and one danger of X-rays. [2 marks]
practice.a: Medical imaging of bones (1); can damage cells and cause cancer (1).

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Ultraviolet and infrared both come from the Sun. Compare their properties, uses and dangers. Portal response box.
independent.a: Both transverse EM waves at the same speed (1); UV higher frequency, shorter wavelength (1); UV use: security marking, sterilising (1); IR use: heating, remote controls (1); UV danger: skin cancer, eye damage (1); IR danger: burns (1).
independent.model: Teacher writes the similarity first: 'Both are electromagnetic waves, transverse, travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): A water wave travels 12 m in 4 s; its wavelength is 1.5 m. Find its frequency.
Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain how people protect themselves from gamma radiation in hospitals.
independent.a: Lead or concrete shielding (1); limit exposure time and keep distance (1).

exit.q: Highest frequency EM wave?
Big question: what do radio, light and X-rays have in common?
exit.a: All are transverse EM waves travelling at the speed of light in a vacuum; they differ in wavelength and frequency.

lessons.homework: Learn the EM spectrum order with a mnemonic; complete the waves quiz on the portal.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled wave diagram; spectrum strip. EAL: amplitude, wavelength, frequency. Stretch: Doppler effect calculations qualitatively.

lessons.bigQuestion: How can light travel along a bent glass fibre?
objectives: To understand reflection, refraction, total internal reflection and sound well enough to answer 4SD0 exam questions
successCriteria: All: state the law of reflection and draw ray diagrams
Most: calculate refractive index from angles
Some: explain total internal reflection and use sin c = 1/n
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: sine and inverse sine
lessons.smsc: Cultural: Ibn al-Haytham's work on refraction and the Book of Optics

keywords.def: n = sin i ÷ sin r
angle of incidence giving a refraction angle of 90°
all light reflected inside a denser medium beyond the critical angle
line at 90° to a surface
thin glass fibre that carries light by total internal reflection

hook.text: A diamond sparkles more than glass cut the same shape. What property of diamond might explain this?
hook.a: Diamond has a higher refractive index and a smaller critical angle, so more light is totally internally reflected.

starter.a: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection

starter.q: Light entering glass bends... the normal.

teach.heading: Refraction
bullets: Practical: glass block, protractor, ray box
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: i = 45°, r = 28°. Find n. [2 marks]

teach.heading: Total internal reflection
bullets: From denser to less dense medium
Angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
teach.note: Uses: optical fibres, prisms in periscopes and binoculars.

teach.heading: Sound
bullets: Longitudinal; can be reflected (echo) and refracted
teach.note: Echo method for speed of sound: distance there and back ÷ time.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Glass with n = 1.5. Critical angle?

practice.q: Calculate the critical angle for water (n = 1.33). [2 marks]
practice.model:
sin c = 1 ÷ n = 1 ÷ 1.33 = 0.752.
Inverse sine: c = 48.8°.

practice.q: State two conditions for total internal reflection. [2 marks]
practice.a: Light travels from a denser to a less dense medium (1); angle of incidence greater than the critical angle (1).

practice.q: Is sound reflected and refracted?
practice.a: Yes: both.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe how to find the refractive index of a glass block. Portal response box.
independent.a: Draw round block, mark normal (1); ray box to shine ray at measured angle i (1); mark emerging ray, join to find refracted ray (1); measure r with protractor (1); repeat for several i (1); calculate sin i ÷ sin r and average, or plot sin i against sin r (1).
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first two points: 'Place the block on paper and draw round it.
Draw a normal at 90° to one face where the ray will enter.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain how an optical fibre carries a signal round a bend.
independent.a: Light enters the fibre (1); hits the inside surface at more than the critical angle (1); is totally internally reflected repeatedly along the fibre (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): A clap echoes from a wall 85 m away after 0.5 s. Calculate the speed of sound.

exit.q: Refractive index formula?
Big question: how can light travel along a bent glass fibre?
exit.a: By total internal reflection: it hits the sides at more than the critical angle and reflects all the way along.

lessons.send: SEND: ray diagram templates with normals; sine table. EAL: refract, critical, normal. Stretch: derive sin c = 1/n from Snell's law.

lessons.title: Practical skills: planning investigations
lessons.bigQuestion: What turns a good idea into a valid experiment?
objectives: To understand how to plan valid investigations and write full-mark method answers
successCriteria: All: identify independent, dependent and control variables
Most: write a method with equipment, steps and measurements
Some: explain how to make results valid, repeatable and safe
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: choosing ranges and intervals
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and care in scientific work

keywords.def: the variable you change
the variable you measure
a variable kept the same
the test measures what it is meant to
the same person gets similar results when repeating

hook.text: A pupil tests five fertilisers on five different plant species. Can she say which fertiliser is best?
hook.a: No: she changed two variables (fertiliser and species), so the test is not valid.

starter.q: The variable you change is the...
Name one control variable in the enzyme temperature practical.
How do you make results more repeatable?
Name one hazard in heating with a Bunsen burner.

teach.heading: The planning checklist
teach.note: Use the diagram as a checklist for 6-mark plans.

teach.heading: Model plan
teach.note: Model a 6-mark plan.

model.problem: Plan an investigation into how temperature affects the rate of osmosis in potato. [6 marks]
steps: Cut equal potato cylinders with a borer; blot and weigh
Place in the same volume and concentration of sucrose solution
Leave for the same time (30 min); blot and reweigh
Calculate % change in mass; repeat three times and find means
Control: cylinder size, solution concentration and volume, time
model.answer: IV, DV, controls, repeats and analysis all included

teach.heading: Validity and errors
teach.note: Use correct terms.

right.title: Systematic error
points: all readings shifted the same way

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: A balance reads 0.2 g with nothing on it. This causes...
check.why: Every reading is shifted by 0.2 g: a zero error, which is systematic.

practice.q: Identify the IV, DV and two controls: 'How does light intensity affect the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed?' [3 marks]
practice.a: IV: light intensity (distance of lamp) (1); DV: bubbles of oxygen per minute (1); controls: temperature, CO₂ concentration, same pondweed (1).
practice.model:
IV: the thing changed: light intensity (lamp distance).
DV: the thing measured: oxygen bubbles per minute.
Controls: anything else that affects rate: temperature, CO₂.

practice.q: Why use a water bath in enzyme practicals? [1 mark]
practice.a: To keep the temperature constant (control).

practice.q: Suggest a suitable range for a temperature investigation on an enzyme.
practice.a: For example 20 to 60 °C in 10 °C steps.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Plan an investigation into how the concentration of acid affects the rate of reaction with magnesium ribbon. Portal response box.
independent.a: IV: acid concentration (range of 5) (1); DV: time to stop fizzing or gas volume in a gas syringe (1); controls: length of Mg, volume of acid, temperature (1); method steps (1); repeat and mean (1); safety: eye protection, acid irritant (1).
independent.model: Teacher writes the variables first, then the first step: 'Measure 25 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid into a conical flask using a measuring cylinder.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why a gas syringe gives more accurate results than counting bubbles.
independent.a: Bubbles vary in size (1); gas syringe measures volume directly (1); smaller resolution, all gas collected (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain the difference between repeatable and reproducible.
independent.a: Repeatable: same person, same method gets similar results (1); reproducible: different people or methods get similar results (1).

exit.q: The variable you measure is the...
Big question: what turns a good idea into a valid experiment?
exit.a: Changing only one variable, measuring the right thing accurately, controlling others, repeating and acting safely.

lessons.send: SEND: planning frame with headings. EAL: variable, control, valid. Stretch: plan for the respiring seeds practical with improvements.

lessons.title: Data skills: tables, graphs and evaluation
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you tell whether a conclusion is really supported by data?
objectives: To understand how to present, analyse and evaluate data in 4SD0 exam questions
successCriteria: All: draw a results table and plot a graph correctly
Most: describe patterns with data and identify anomalies
Some: evaluate data, calculate gradients and justify conclusions
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: graphs, means and gradients
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest use of evidence

keywords.def: a result that does not fit the pattern
sum of values ÷ number of values
line or curve showing the trend
a relationship between two variables
smallest change an instrument can show

hook.text: A graph of ice cream sales and sunburn cases goes up together. Does ice cream cause sunburn?
hook.a: No: both are caused by hot sunny weather. Correlation is not causation.

starter.q: Mean of 12, 14, 13 and 25 (25 is an anomaly)?
Which axis for the independent variable?

starter.a: Change in y ÷ change in x

teach.heading: Tables and graphs
bullets: Units in headings, not in cells
IV on the x-axis, DV on y
Use over half the grid; plot ±½ square
teach.note: Model a full-mark graph.

teach.heading: Describe, then explain
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Describe the trend in the table. [2 marks]
steps: As concentration increases, the mean time decreases
Use data: from 86 s at 0.2 mol/dm³ to 23 s at 0.8 mol/dm³

teach.heading: Evaluate
bullets: Is the conclusion only for this range?
teach.note: Evaluation vocabulary.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which value is anomalous?
check.why: 52 s is far from the other 0.6 mol/dm³ result (30 s) and breaks the trend.

practice.q: Calculate the mean at 0.6 mol/dm³ excluding the anomaly. [1 mark]
practice.model:
Identify the anomaly: 52 s.
Exclude it.
Only 30 s remains (a third repeat would be needed), so mean = 30 s.

practice.q: Explain the trend using collision theory. [2 marks]
practice.a: Higher concentration: more particles in the same volume (1), more frequent successful collisions so faster reaction (1).

practice.q: A thermometer reads to 1 °C. What is its resolution?

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Plot the mean data (portal graph grid), draw a curve of best fit, describe the trend and identify the anomaly.
independent.a: Axes labelled with units (1); scale over half grid (1); points correct (1); smooth curve (1); trend: time decreases as concentration increases (1); 52 s anomaly identified (1).
independent.model: Teacher draws the axes first: x: concentration (mol/dm³), 0 to 1.0; y: mean time (s), 0 to 100; plots the first point (0.2, 86).

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 2 marks): Calculate rate as 1000 ÷ mean time at 0.4 and 0.8 mol/dm³. What happens when concentration doubles?
independent.a: 22.7 and 43.5 s⁻¹ (1); the rate roughly doubles (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 3 marks): Evaluate the conclusion 'Doubling concentration always doubles the rate'.
independent.a: Data roughly support it for this range (1); only two repeats, one anomaly (1); cannot extend beyond 0.8 mol/dm³ or other temperatures (1).

exit.q: A result that does not fit the pattern is...
Big question: how can you tell whether a conclusion is supported?
exit.a: Check the trend is clear across the range, repeats agree, anomalies are dealt with, and the science explains it.

lessons.send: SEND: graph with axes drawn. EAL: trend, anomaly, evaluate. Stretch: calculate a gradient from a tangent on a curve.

objectives: To understand the 4SD0 chemistry practicals well enough to describe and evaluate them in exams
successCriteria: All: name the practicals and their purpose
Most: describe the steps of chromatography, salt preparation and the metal oxide formula
Some: identify errors and improvements in each practical
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: chromatography in food and medicine testing
lessons.smsc: Moral: safety and care for others in practical work

keywords.def: separating dissolved substances by movement through paper
forming crystals from a saturated solution
more than enough so all of the other reactant is used
heating until mass stops changing
safety glasses or goggles

hook.text: When heating magnesium in a crucible, why lift the lid only a little and only now and then?
hook.a: To let oxygen in while stopping magnesium oxide smoke escaping and losing mass.

starter.a: Distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent

starter.q: Why use pencil for the chromatography start line?
starter.a: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent
options: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent

starter.q: Why add copper oxide in excess when making copper sulfate?
starter.a: To use up all the acid

teach.heading: The practicals
bullets: Chromatography of inks or food colourings
Oxygen in air; acids with metals
teach.note: Spec practical list.

teach.heading: Heating to constant mass
bullets: Repeat until the mass stays the same
teach.note: Used in the metal oxide practical.

teach.heading: Model answer
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: A student's magnesium oxide formula came out as Mg₃O₂ (too little oxygen). Suggest two reasons. [2 marks]
steps: Not all magnesium reacted: not heated to constant mass
Some magnesium oxide smoke escaped when the lid was lifted

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Why should copper sulfate solution not be boiled to dryness?
options: Hydrated crystals would lose their water of crystallisation
check.why: Boiling to dryness gives white anhydrous powder, not blue hydrated crystals.

practice.q: Describe how to carry out paper chromatography of food colourings. [4 marks]
practice.a: Pencil line near the bottom (1); spots of colourings on the line (1); stand in solvent below the line, lid on (1); remove when solvent near top, mark solvent front, dry (1).
practice.model: Four steps, four marks: pencil line, spots, solvent below the line with a lid, mark the front and dry.

practice.q: Why is the solvent level below the start line? [1 mark]
practice.a: So the spots do not dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.

practice.q: State one safety precaution when heating magnesium. [1 mark]
practice.a: Eye protection; do not look directly at the flame; use tongs; heatproof mat.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Describe how to find the empirical formula of magnesium oxide by experiment. Portal response box.
independent.a: Weigh crucible and lid (1); add Mg ribbon, weigh (1); heat strongly, lifting lid occasionally (1); heat to constant mass (1); cool and weigh (1); calculate masses of Mg and O and convert to moles (1).
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first two points: 'Weigh an empty crucible and lid.
Add a coiled piece of cleaned magnesium ribbon and weigh again.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Describe how to show that a sample of water is pure.
independent.a: Heat and measure the boiling point (1); pure water boils at exactly 100 °C (1) at standard pressure; (freezes at 0 °C) (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): Explain why the volume of air decreases when iron wool rusts in an enclosed tube.
independent.a: Iron reacts with oxygen (1), removing it from the air, so the gas volume falls by about 21% (1).

exit.q: Heating to constant mass shows...
Big question: what do examiners look for in a practical method answer?
exit.a: Clear ordered steps, named equipment, what is measured and how, controls, and safety.

lessons.title: Revision: Physics 4 energy stores, efficiency and thermal transfer
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a vacuum flask keep tea hot for hours?
objectives: To understand energy transfers, efficiency and thermal energy transfer well enough to answer 4SD0 exam questions
successCriteria: All: describe energy transfers and draw Sankey diagrams
Most: calculate efficiency
Some: explain conduction, convection and radiation and how insulation reduces them
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: home energy use and insulation
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding waste of energy

keywords.def: useful energy output ÷ total energy output × 100%
transfer through a solid by particle vibrations (and free electrons in metals)
transfer by movement of a fluid as warmer, less dense fluid rises
transfer by infrared waves; no medium needed
diagram showing energy transfers with arrow widths

hook.text: A shiny silver survival blanket keeps a person warm though it is very thin. How?
hook.a: It reflects infrared radiation back and reduces convection.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Do not squander wastefully' (al-Isra 17:26). Efficiency and insulation are scientific ways of reducing waste.

starter.q: Efficiency of a lamp: 20 J light from 100 J?
Name the energy store in food.
Hot air rises because it is...

teach.heading: Efficiency
bullets: Wasted energy is usually dissipated as heat
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: A motor is supplied with 200 J and does 150 J of useful work. Efficiency? [2 marks]

teach.heading: Thermal transfer
bullets: Radiation: infrared, dark matt surfaces emit and absorb best
teach.note: Vacuum flask.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Exam trap.

misconception.wrong: Heat rises
misconception.right: Warmer fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; this is convection

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Best emitter of infrared radiation?
check.why: Dark matt surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers.

practice.q: A TV uses 120 J; 30 J is light and sound. Efficiency? [2 marks]
practice.model:
Useful output: 30 J.
Total: 120 J.
Efficiency = 30 ÷ 120 × 100 = 25%.

practice.q: Explain why radiators are near the floor. [2 marks]
practice.a: Air near the radiator warms, becomes less dense and rises (1), setting up a convection current that heats the room (1).

practice.q: Why do pans have copper bases? [1 mark]
practice.a: Copper is a good thermal conductor.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Explain how a vacuum flask reduces energy transfer by conduction, convection and radiation. Portal response box.
independent.a: Vacuum: no particles, so no conduction (1) or convection (1) across the gap; silvered walls reflect infrared (1), reducing radiation (1); stopper reduces convection and evaporation from the top (1); plastic is an insulator (1).
independent.model: Teacher writes the first point: 'The vacuum between the walls has no particles, so energy cannot be transferred across it by conduction.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Describe an experiment to compare the infrared emitted by different surfaces (Leslie cube or cans of hot water).
independent.a: Cans painted different colours, same volume of hot water (1); measure temperature drop over the same time (1); fastest cooling is the best emitter (matt black) (1).

independent.q: Stretch (exam-style, 2 marks): A device is 40% efficient and wastes 300 J. What was the total input?
independent.a: Wasted energy is 60% of the input (1); input = 300 ÷ 0.6 = 500 J (1)

exit.q: Efficiency can never be more than...
Big question: why does a vacuum flask keep tea hot for hours?
exit.a: The vacuum stops conduction and convection and the silvered walls reduce radiation.

keywords.def: a different form of the same gene
allele expressed when one copy is present

two identical alleles

hook.text: Two parents with brown eyes have a blue-eyed child. How is that possible?
hook.a: Both are heterozygous (Bb); each passes on b, so the child is bb.

starter.q: A gene codes for a specific...

steps: Gametes: T, t and T, t
Punnett square: TT, Tt, Tt, tt

teach.heading: Pedigrees (spec 3.24)
bullets: Two unaffected parents with an affected child: recessive, both carriers
teach.note: Work from the affected children.

check.q: Cross Bb × bb. Probability of bb?
