practice.q: Cystic fibrosis is recessive (f). Two carriers (Ff) have a child. Probability the child has CF? [3 marks]
practice.a: Gametes F, f from each (1); Punnett FF, Ff, Ff, ff (1); 1 in 4, 25% (1)
practice.model: Carriers are Ff. Each gives F or f. Square: FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Only ff has CF: 1 out of 4.

practice.q: Define phenotype.

practice.q: Why is the chance of a boy always 50%?
practice.a: The father's sperm carry X or Y in equal numbers

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 7 marks): Pedigree on the sheet (two unaffected parents, one affected son). (a) Is the allele dominant or recessive? Explain [2]. (b) Give the parents' genotypes [2]. (c) Draw a Punnett square for the next child and give the probability it is unaffected [3].
independent.a: (a) recessive (1): unaffected parents had an affected child, so both carry the allele (1); (b) both Aa (2); (c) AA, Aa, Aa, aa (2); 3/4 or 75% unaffected (1)
independent.model: Teacher sets out (a): 'Recessive, because...'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why most human features show a range of phenotypes.
independent.a: Most features are polygenic (1), controlled by several genes (1), and also affected by the environment (1)

independent.q: Stretch (2 marks): Two tall plants give 75 tall and 25 dwarf offspring. What were the parents' genotypes? Explain.
independent.a: Both Tt (1): a 3:1 ratio shows both parents carry the recessive allele (1)

exit.q: Heterozygous means...
Big question: how do brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child?
exit.a: Both are heterozygous; each passes the recessive allele.

independent.q: Stretch: Draw a reaction profile with and without a catalyst and label activation energy.
independent.a: Lower hump for catalysed path; same start and end energies

keywords.def: mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V
force per unit area, p = F/A
temperature scale starting at absolute zero
gas pressure is caused by molecules colliding with walls

hook.text: A sealed crisp packet puffs up on a mountain road and a plastic bottle crumples after a flight lands. What links them?
hook.a: Pressure differences: lower outside pressure lets the gas inside expand; higher outside pressure crushes the bottle.

teach.heading: Equations (spec 5.3, 5.5, 5.7, 5.21, 5.22)
teach.note: Temperature must be in kelvin for gas laws.

teach.heading: Pressure in a liquid
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

teach.heading: Gas law
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

teach.heading: Kinetic theory (spec 5.15, 5.18 to 5.20)
bullets: Molecules move randomly, hit walls: pressure
Higher T: faster molecules, harder and more frequent collisions
Smaller V at constant T: more frequent collisions
teach.note: Kelvin T ∝ mean kinetic energy.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: A gas at 200 kPa in 3.0 L is compressed to 1.5 L at constant temperature. New pressure?
check.why: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂: 200 × 3.0 = p₂ × 1.5, so p₂ = 400 kPa.

practice.q: A stone has mass 270 g and displaces 100 cm³ of water. Density? [2 marks]
practice.model: Density = mass ÷ volume. Volume from displacement = 100 cm³. 270 ÷ 100 = 2.7 g/cm³.

practice.q: A 600 N force on 0.02 m². Pressure?
Convert 0 K to °C.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 8 marks): (a) Describe how to find the density of an irregular object [3]. (b) A diver is at 12 m in sea water (ρ = 1030 kg/m³). Calculate the extra pressure [2]. (c) A bubble of 2.0 cm³ at that depth (total pressure 224 kPa) rises to the surface (100 kPa). Calculate its new volume at constant temperature [3].
independent.a: (a) mass on a balance (1); volume by displacement in a measuring cylinder or eureka can (1); ρ = m ÷ V (1); (b) p = 12 × 1030 × 10 = 123 600 Pa (2); (c) p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (1); 224 × 2.0 = 100 × V₂ (1); V₂ = 4.48 cm³ (1)
independent.model: Teacher sets out (b): equation, substitution, answer with unit.

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain, using particles, why the pressure in a tyre rises on a hot day.
independent.a: Air molecules gain kinetic energy/move faster (1); collide with walls more often (1) and with more force (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why must temperatures be in kelvin for p/T = constant?
independent.a: Pressure is proportional to absolute temperature; °C has an arbitrary zero.

exit.q: For gas laws, temperature must be in...
Big question: why does the crisp packet puff up on a mountain?
exit.a: Outside pressure is lower, so the gas inside expands.

lessons.title: Revision: B3 cell division, variation and natural selection
lessons.bigQuestion: Doctors warn: finish the whole course of antibiotics. How could stopping early help bacteria 'win'?
objectives: To understand mitosis, meiosis, variation, mutation and natural selection well enough to answer 4SD0 questions
successCriteria: All: compare mitosis and meiosis

keywords.def: cell division giving two genetically identical diploid cells
cell division giving four genetically different haploid gametes
a rare, random change in genetic material that can be inherited
individuals better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more
bacteria no longer killed by an antibiotic

hook.text: Doctors warn: finish the whole course of antibiotics. How could stopping early help bacteria 'win'?
hook.a: Surviving bacteria may include resistant ones, which reproduce and pass on resistance.

islamicLink.text: The Islamic position: Muslims believe Allah created Adam (peace be upon him) directly from clay: 'We created man from sounding clay, from altered black mud' (Al-Hijr 15:26), and Allah says He created him 'with My hands' (Sad 38:75). So Muslims do not accept that human beings descended from earlier animals. Change within living things that can be observed, such as bacteria becoming resistant, happens by Allah's decree. For the exam, explain Darwin's theory accurately as the specification asks; knowing a theory is not the same as believing it.

starter.q: Mitosis is used for growth and...

teach.heading: Mitosis vs meiosis (spec 3.28 to 3.32)
teach.note: Learn the numbers.

teach.heading: Variation and mutation (spec 3.33, 3.34)
bullets: Most have no effect; some harmful; rarely beneficial
teach.note: Random fertilisation adds variation (3.31).

teach.heading: Natural selection (spec 3.38)
bullets: Alleles passed on; frequency rises over generations
teach.note: Darwin's theory: learn it accurately for the exam.

teach.heading: Antibiotic resistance (spec 3.39)
bullets: Mutation gives resistance in a few bacteria
teach.note: Finish courses; avoid unnecessary prescriptions.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Why do resistant bacteria increase?
options: Non-resistant bacteria are killed, resistant ones survive and reproduce
check.why: The antibiotic is the selection pressure; it does not cause the mutation.

practice.q: Explain how antibiotic resistance spreads in a population of bacteria. [4 marks]
practice.a: Random mutation gives resistance (1); antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria (1); resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (1); pass on the resistance allele/population becomes resistant (1)
practice.model: Four links: mutation, selection by antibiotic, survival and reproduction, inheritance.

practice.q: State two differences between mitosis and meiosis.
practice.a: Mitosis 2 cells, meiosis 4; mitosis identical, meiosis different (or diploid vs haploid)

practice.q: Give an example of environmental variation.
practice.a: Scars, language, a plant's height in poor soil

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 6 marks): Explain how a population of insects becomes resistant to a pesticide. Portal response box.
independent.a: Variation in the population (1); due to a mutation (1); pesticide kills non-resistant insects (1); resistant insects survive (1); reproduce and pass on the allele (1); over many generations most are resistant (1)
independent.model: Teacher writes the first point: 'There is variation in the insect population caused by mutation.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Why is meiosis needed before fertilisation?
independent.a: Halves the chromosome number (1) so the zygote has the normal diploid number (1); produces variation (1)

independent.q: Stretch (2 marks): Suggest two ways hospitals reduce antibiotic resistance.
independent.a: Prescribe only when needed; patients finish courses; hygiene to stop spread

exit.q: Meiosis produces ... cells.
Big question: how could stopping antibiotics early help bacteria?
exit.a: Resistant survivors reproduce and pass resistance on.

lessons.homework: Complete the B3 cell division and natural selection exam set on the portal (timed, 25 minutes).
lessons.send: SEND: mitosis and meiosis table to complete. EAL: mutation, selection. Stretch: explain why variation is vital for natural selection.

Some: describe the carbon cycle and the quadrat practical
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: ecosystems and biomes
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: balance in creation (al-mizan)

keywords.def: all the organisms of one species in an area
all the populations in an area
a community and its physical environment
a feeding level in a food chain
a square frame used to sample organisms

hook.text: Why are there no lion-eating predators in the savanna?
hook.a: Energy is lost at each trophic level, so there is not enough left to support another level.

teach.heading: Definitions (spec 4.1, 4.5)
teach.note: Use the words exactly.

teach.heading: Food chains and pyramids (spec 4.6 to 4.9)
teach.note: Energy lost in respiration, movement, heat, faeces and uneaten parts.

chart.title: Energy at each trophic level (example, kJ/m²/year)

teach.heading: Carbon cycle (spec 4.10)
bullets: Respiration, decomposition and combustion return CO₂
teach.note: Fossil fuels form from dead remains over millions of years.

teach.heading: Quadrats (spec 4.2)
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: 10 quadrats (each 0.25 m²) in a 100 m² field find 2, 4, 3, 1, 0, 2, 5, 3, 2, 3 daisies. Estimate the population.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Energy transfer efficiency from 5000 kJ to 450 kJ is...

practice.q: Explain why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient. [3 marks]
practice.a: Energy used in respiration/lost as heat (1); not all parts eaten (bones, roots) (1); energy lost in faeces/urine (1)
practice.model: Three losses: respiration and heat, uneaten parts, and waste. Name each one.

practice.q: State two processes that release CO₂ into the air.
practice.a: Respiration, combustion (or decomposition)

practice.q: Why are quadrats placed randomly?
practice.a: To avoid bias and give a representative sample

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 7 marks): (a) Describe how to compare the population of dandelions on a sunny and a shady lawn using quadrats [4]. (b) Calculate the efficiency of transfer from grass (20 000 kJ) to rabbits (1600 kJ) [2]. (c) Name one abiotic factor that could explain a difference in the dandelion results [1].
independent.a: (a) random coordinates/quadrats in each area (1); same size and number of quadrats (1); count dandelions in each (1); calculate mean per quadrat and compare (1); (b) 1600 ÷ 20 000 × 100 = 8% (2); (c) light intensity (or water, temperature) (1)
independent.model: Teacher sets out (a): 'Use a random number table to place 10 quadrats in each area.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain how carbon in a rabbit's body can end up in a plant.
independent.a: Rabbit dies and is decomposed by microorganisms (1); they respire, releasing CO₂ (1); plants absorb CO₂ in photosynthesis (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why are pyramids of biomass usually pyramid-shaped but pyramids of number not always?
independent.a: One large producer (e.g. a tree) supports many consumers, but its biomass is still greater.

exit.q: A community is all the ... in an area.
Big question: why no lion-eating predators?
exit.a: Too little energy reaches that trophic level to support it.

lessons.title: Revision: C3 energetics and reversible reactions
lessons.bigQuestion: Hand warmers get hot and instant ice packs go cold. How could you compare them in numbers, not just 'hot' and 'cold'?
objectives: To understand calorimetry, enthalpy change and reversible reactions well enough to answer 4SD0 calculations
successCriteria: All: use Q = mcΔT
Most: calculate molar enthalpy change ΔH with the correct sign
Some: describe two reversible reactions
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging formulae
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest reporting of experimental error

keywords.def: gives out heat energy; ΔH negative
takes in heat energy; ΔH positive
measuring heat energy change using a temperature change
heat energy change per mole, ΔH in kJ/mol
a reaction that can go both ways, shown by ⇌

hook.text: Hand warmers get hot and instant ice packs go cold. How could you compare them in numbers, not just 'hot' and 'cold'?
hook.a: Measure the temperature change of a known mass of water, calculate Q = mcΔT, then ΔH per mole.

teach.heading: Calorimetry (spec 3.1, 3.2, 3.8)
bullets: Measure ΔT of a known mass of solution or water
teach.note: Assume 1 cm³ of solution = 1 g and c = 4.2 J/g °C.

teach.heading: Q and ΔH (spec 3.3, 3.4)
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: 50 g of acid and alkali solution rises by 12 °C when 0.020 mol of water forms. Find ΔH.

teach.heading: Errors
bullets: Heat lost to surroundings: ΔT too small
Use a lid and insulated cup
teach.note: Answers are usually less exothermic than data-book values.

teach.heading: Reversible reactions (spec 3.17, 3.18)
bullets: One direction exothermic, the other endothermic
teach.note: Equilibrium is Chemistry-only: not in 4SD0.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: A dissolving makes the temperature fall by 5 °C. ΔH is...
check.why: Temperature falls: heat taken in, endothermic, positive ΔH.

practice.q: 100 g water heated by 8.0 °C. Q? [2 marks]
Water added to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. What do you see and is it exo- or endothermic?
practice.a: Turns blue and gets hot: exothermic

practice.q: Why use a polystyrene cup?
practice.a: Insulator: reduces heat loss

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 8 marks): 0.50 g of magnesium (0.0208 mol) reacts with excess copper(II) sulfate solution (50 cm³). The temperature rises from 21.0 °C to 46.0 °C. (a) Calculate Q [2]. (b) Calculate ΔH in kJ/mol [3]. (c) Give two reasons the value is less exothermic than the data-book value [2]. (d) State the sign of ΔH and why [1].
independent.a: (a) Q = 50 × 4.2 × 25 = 5250 J (2); (b) 5.25 kJ ÷ 0.0208 (1) = 252 (1); ΔH = -252 kJ/mol (1); (c) heat lost to surroundings; not all Mg reacted or heat absorbed by the cup (2); (d) negative: exothermic, temperature rose (1)
independent.model: Teacher sets out (a): ΔT = 46.0 - 21.0 = 25.0 °C.

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why heating blue copper(II) sulfate is endothermic but adding water to the white solid is exothermic.
independent.a: Reversible reaction (1); same energy transferred in each direction (1); in opposite directions: taken in when heated, given out when water added (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Calculate the mass of water heated by 21 000 J with ΔT = 50 °C.

exit.q: ΔH for an exothermic reaction is...
Big question: how could you compare hand warmers and ice packs in numbers?
exit.a: Measure ΔT of known mass, Q = mcΔT, then ΔH per mole.

lessons.send: SEND: Q = mcΔT card. EAL: exothermic, endothermic, enthalpy. Stretch: compare calorimetry of fuels.

lessons.title: Revision: P6 magnetism and electromagnetism
lessons.bigQuestion: A motor and a generator are almost the same machine. What is the difference in what goes in and what comes out?
objectives: To understand magnetic fields, the motor effect and electromagnetic induction well enough to answer 4SD0 questions
successCriteria: All: draw field patterns for magnets and wires
Most: use the left-hand rule and state how to increase the force
Some: explain how a generator induces a voltage
lessons.crossCurricular: DT: motors in products
lessons.smsc: Social: electricity generation for everyone

keywords.def: region where a magnetic material or wire feels a force
easily magnetised and demagnetised, e.g. iron
force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field
voltage induced when a conductor cuts field lines or the field changes
thumb motion, first finger field, second finger current

hook.text: A motor and a generator are almost the same machine. What is the difference in what goes in and what comes out?
hook.a: Motor: current in, movement out. Generator: movement in, induced voltage out.

starter.q: Is steel magnetically hard or soft?

teach.heading: Magnets (spec 6.2 to 6.7)
bullets: Uniform field between flat opposite poles
Plotting compass practical for field patterns
teach.note: Field lines never cross.

teach.heading: Current and fields (spec 6.8)
bullets: A wire with current has a circular field
Coil: field like a bar magnet
teach.note: Electromagnets switch on and off.

teach.heading: Motor effect (spec 6.12 to 6.14)
bullets: Force when current is at 90° to field
Bigger current or stronger field: bigger force
teach.note: Reverse current or field: force reverses. Used in motors and loudspeakers.

teach.heading: Induction (spec 6.15, 6.16)
bullets: Move wire across field: voltage induced
Faster, stronger field, more turns: bigger voltage
Rotating magnet in a coil (or coil in field): a.c. generator
teach.note: No movement, no induced voltage.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: How can you increase the force on a wire in a field?
options: Make the wire parallel to the field
check.why: Force increases with field strength and current; parallel gives no force.

practice.q: Explain how a loudspeaker produces sound. [3 marks]
practice.a: Alternating current in the coil in a magnetic field (1); force on coil changes direction (motor effect) (1); cone vibrates, making pressure waves (sound) (1)
practice.model: Current in a field gives a force. Alternating current reverses the force many times a second. The cone vibrates: sound.

practice.q: State two ways to increase the induced voltage in a generator.
practice.a: Rotate faster; stronger magnet; more turns on the coil

practice.q: Why is iron used in an electromagnet core?
practice.a: It is magnetically soft: magnetises strongly and demagnetises when switched off

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 7 marks): (a) Draw the field around a single bar magnet [2]. (b) Describe how to use a plotting compass to find the field pattern [2]. (c) A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a meter. Describe and explain the meter reading when the magnet is pushed in, held still, and pulled out [3].
independent.a: (a) lines N to S, curved, not crossing, arrows (2); (b) place compass at N pole, mark needle direction, move along, join dots (2); (c) pushed in: deflection (1); still: zero, no change in field (1); pulled out: opposite deflection (1)
independent.model: Teacher draws the bar magnet and the first field line with an arrow.

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why the coil of a d.c. motor rotates continuously in one direction.
independent.a: Forces on opposite sides act in opposite directions, giving a turning effect (1); split-ring commutator reverses current every half turn (1), keeping the force in the same rotational sense (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why does a bicycle dynamo light dim when you ride slowly?
independent.a: Slower rotation cuts field lines more slowly, inducing a smaller voltage.

exit.q: A motor changes electrical energy into...
Big question: difference between a motor and a generator?
exit.a: Motor: current in, movement out; generator: movement in, voltage out.

lessons.homework: Complete the P6 exam set on the portal (timed, 25 minutes).
lessons.send: SEND: left-hand rule card. EAL: field, induce, rotate. Stretch: explain why a.c. generators produce alternating voltage.

lessons.title: Revision: B5 use of biological resources
lessons.bigQuestion: People with diabetes once used insulin from pigs and cows; now most is made by bacteria. How can a bacterium make a human protein?
objectives: To understand how humans use plants, microorganisms and genetic technology to produce food and medicines
successCriteria: All: explain how glasshouses, CO₂, temperature and fertilisers raise yield
Most: describe yeast, Lactobacillus and fermenters
Some: describe selective breeding and genetic modification of bacteria
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: food security and farming
lessons.smsc: Moral: ethics of genetic technology

keywords.def: the amount of crop produced
using a predator or parasite to control a pest
a vessel for growing microorganisms on a large scale
choosing parents with desired features to breed over many generations
containing genes transferred from another species

hook.text: People with diabetes once used insulin from pigs and cows; now most is made by bacteria. How can a bacterium make a human protein?
hook.a: The human insulin gene is cut out with restriction enzymes, inserted into a plasmid with ligase, and the bacterium makes insulin in a fermenter.

starter.q: Yeast respires anaerobically to make ethanol and...

teach.heading: Crops (spec 5.1 to 5.4)
bullets: Glasshouses and polytunnels: warmth, extra CO₂, longer season
Pest control: pesticides vs biological control
teach.note: Evaluate: biological control is specific but slower; pesticides fast but can harm other species and build up.

teach.heading: Microorganisms (spec 5.5 to 5.8)
bullets: Fermenter: aseptic, nutrients, temperature, pH, oxygen, stirring
teach.note: Aseptic: prevents contamination.

teach.heading: Genetic modification (spec 5.12 to 5.16)
bullets: Restriction enzyme cuts the gene and plasmid
Bacteria in fermenter make human insulin
teach.note: GM crops: pest or herbicide resistance, more nutrients.

timeline.text: Cut insulin gene out with restriction enzyme
Cut plasmid with the same enzyme

teach.heading: Selective breeding (spec 5.10, 5.11)
bullets: Choose parents with the desired feature
teach.note: Reduces variation: risk of disease and inherited defects.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Why are fermenters kept aseptic?
options: To prevent contamination by unwanted microorganisms
check.why: Other microbes would compete or spoil the product.

practice.q: Explain why adding CO₂ to a glasshouse can increase yield. [2 marks]
practice.a: CO₂ is a limiting factor for photosynthesis (1); more CO₂, faster photosynthesis, more glucose for growth (1)
practice.model: What limits photosynthesis? CO₂ can. Raise it: faster photosynthesis, more sugar, more growth.

practice.q: What does Lactobacillus produce in yoghurt making?
practice.a: Lactic acid

practice.q: Name the enzyme that joins DNA.
practice.a: Ligase

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 8 marks): (a) Describe how bacteria are genetically modified to produce human insulin [4]. (b) Explain two conditions that must be controlled in an industrial fermenter [4].
independent.a: (a) restriction enzyme cuts out the insulin gene (1) and opens the plasmid (1); ligase joins gene into plasmid (1); plasmid inserted into bacteria, which make insulin (1); (b) any two with reasons: temperature, optimum for enzymes (2); pH, optimum for enzymes (2); oxygen for aerobic respiration (2); aseptic to avoid contamination (2); nutrients for growth (2)
independent.model: Teacher writes the first point: 'A restriction enzyme cuts the human insulin gene out of the DNA.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Evaluate biological control of greenhouse whitefly using a parasitic wasp.
independent.a: Specific, no chemical residue, self-sustaining (1, 1); but slower and may not eliminate the pest/wasp could escape (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Give one risk of selective breeding.
independent.a: Reduced gene pool, so more vulnerable to new diseases or inherited defects.

exit.q: Restriction enzymes ... DNA.
Big question: how can a bacterium make a human protein?
exit.a: The human gene is inserted into its plasmid; the bacterium follows the gene's code.

lessons.send: SEND: GM steps cards to order. EAL: plasmid, vector, ferment. Stretch: discuss ethical issues of GM crops.

keywords.def: compound of hydrogen and carbon only
family with the same general formula and functional group
same molecular formula, different structural formula
only single C-C bonds
contains a C=C double bond

hook.text: Petrol, diesel and bitumen all come from the same black liquid. How are they separated?
hook.a: Fractional distillation: fractions with different boiling points condense at different heights in a column.

starter.q: Bromine water with an alkene turns...

teach.heading: Formulae and naming (spec 4.1 to 4.5)
teach.note: Ethane C₂H₆, empirical CH₃.

teach.heading: Fractional distillation (spec 4.7 to 4.10)
teach.note: Bottom: long chains, high boiling point, viscous, dark.

head: Fraction
Use
rows: fuel for some cars and trains
fuel for ships and power stations

teach.heading: Alkanes (spec 4.19 to 4.22)
bullets: Combustion; substitution with halogens in UV
teach.note: Mono-substitution only for 4SD0.

teach.heading: Alkenes (spec 4.23 to 4.28)
bullets: Addition with bromine: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂
teach.note: Alkanes leave bromine water orange.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Which is an alkene?
check.why: C₄H₈ fits CₙH₂ₙ: butene.

practice.q: Draw the two structural isomers of C₄H₁₀ and name them. [3 marks]
practice.a: Butane (straight chain) (1); methylpropane (branched) (1); correct displayed formulae (1)
practice.model: Four carbons in a line: butane. Three in a line with one branching off the middle: methylpropane. Same formula, different structure.

practice.q: Write the equation for ethene with bromine.
practice.a: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂

practice.q: Why does bitumen have a high boiling point?
practice.a: Long-chain molecules with strong intermolecular forces

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 8 marks): (a) Describe how crude oil is separated into fractions [4]. (b) Describe a test to distinguish propane from propene, with results [3]. (c) Give the name of C₅H₁₂ [1].
independent.a: (a) crude oil heated/vaporised (1); vapour rises up column, cooler at top (1); fractions condense at their boiling points (1); short chains/low bp collected at top, long at bottom (1); (b) add bromine water and shake (1); propene: orange to colourless (1); propane: stays orange (1); (c) pentane (1)
independent.model: Teacher writes the first point: 'Crude oil is heated until most of it vaporises.'

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 2 marks): Write the equation for methane reacting with chlorine in UV light and name the type of reaction.
independent.a: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (1); substitution (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why alkanes are called saturated.
independent.a: Each carbon has the maximum number of hydrogen atoms; only single bonds, no C=C.

exit.q: Alkenes decolourise bromine water by...
Big question: how are petrol and bitumen separated?

lessons.title: Revision: P7 radioactivity and half-life
lessons.bigQuestion: A source has an activity of 800 Bq today. Why can't anyone predict which atom will decay next, yet we can say what the activity will be in 6 hours?
objectives: To understand atomic structure, the three radiations, nuclear equations and half-life well enough to answer 4SD0 questions
successCriteria: All: compare alpha, beta and gamma radiation
Most: balance nuclear equations
Some: calculate half-life from data and graphs
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: halving and exponential decay
lessons.smsc: Moral: safe use of radiation in medicine

keywords.def: atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
two protons and two neutrons (helium nucleus)
a fast electron from the nucleus
time for the activity (or number of unstable nuclei) to halve
unit of activity: one decay per second

hook.text: A source has an activity of 800 Bq today. Why can't anyone predict which atom will decay next, yet we can say what the activity will be in 6 hours?
hook.a: Decay is random for each nucleus, but with huge numbers the half-life gives a reliable average.

teach.heading: The radiations (spec 7.4 to 7.6)
teach.note: Learn the table.

head: Radiation
Nature
Stopped by
Ionising
rows: paper or a few cm of air

teach.heading: Nuclear equations (spec 7.7, 7.8)
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: Radium-226 (proton number 88) emits an alpha particle. Write the equation.

teach.heading: Half-life (spec 7.12, 7.13)
teach.note: I do: talk through each step.

model.problem: Activity 800 Bq, half-life 2 hours. Find the activity after 6 hours.

teach.heading: Uses and dangers (spec 7.9, 7.10, 7.14 to 7.16)
bullets: Background: rocks, radon, cosmic rays, medical
Uses: tracers, smoke alarms (alpha), sterilising (gamma), thickness control (beta)
teach.note: Detect with a Geiger-Müller tube or photographic film.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Beta decay changes the proton number by...
check.why: A neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted, so proton number rises by 1; mass number unchanged.

practice.q: Carbon-14 (proton number 6) decays by beta emission. Write the equation. [2 marks]
practice.a: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e (products 1, balanced 1)
practice.model: Beta: mass stays 14, proton number goes up 1 to 7: nitrogen. Add the electron ⁰₋₁e.

practice.q: Which radiation is used in smoke alarms and why?
practice.a: Alpha: strongly ionising, short range, stopped by smoke

practice.q: A count falls from 360 to 45 counts/min in 30 min. Half-life?
practice.a: 10 min (3 half-lives)

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 8 marks): (a) Describe an experiment with a source, a GM tube and absorbers to identify the radiation emitted [3]. (b) Graph on the sheet: find the half-life [2]. (c) Explain why gamma is used to sterilise surgical instruments but alpha is not [2]. (d) Distinguish contamination from irradiation [1].
independent.a: (a) measure background count (1); measure count with paper, then aluminium, then lead between source and tube (1); where the count drops to background identifies the type (1); (b) read time for activity to halve, e.g. 40 s (2); (c) gamma penetrates packaging and kills microbes (1); alpha cannot pass through packaging (1); (d) contamination: source on or in the object; irradiation: exposed to radiation from outside (1)
independent.model: Teacher sets out (b) on the graph: start at 600, halve to 300, read across and down.

independent.q: Extend (exam-style, 3 marks): Explain why alpha sources are most dangerous inside the body but least dangerous outside.
independent.a: Strongly ionising so damages cells inside (1); outside, stopped by dead skin/air (1); inside, nothing stops it reaching living cells (1)

independent.q: Stretch: A sample has 1/16 of its original activity after 20 years. Find the half-life.
independent.a: 1/16 = 4 half-lives, so 5 years.

exit.q: Half-life is the time for activity to...
Big question: how can we predict activity if decay is random?
exit.a: With huge numbers of nuclei, half-life gives a reliable average.

lessons.title: Revision: B4 human impact, then a timed B3 to B5 section
lessons.bigQuestion: A farmer's fertiliser can kill fish in a river a kilometre away. Trace the chain of events.
objectives: To understand pollution and the greenhouse effect and to apply B3 to B5 knowledge under timed conditions

Most: explain the enhanced greenhouse effect

lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: climate change and pollution
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship (khilafah) of the earth

keywords.def: excess nutrients cause algal growth, oxygen depletion and death of aquatic life
absorbs infrared radiation: water vapour, CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs
rain made acidic by SO₂ and nitrogen oxides
toxic gas that binds to haemoglobin
rise in average global temperature

hook.text: A farmer's fertiliser can kill fish in a river a kilometre away. Trace the chain of events.
hook.a: Fertiliser leaches into the river; algae bloom; algae die; bacteria decompose them and use up oxygen; fish suffocate.

starter.q: About ...% of energy passes to the next trophic level.
Name a greenhouse gas from cattle.
Half-life of 2 h: 800 Bq after 4 h?

teach.heading: Air pollution (spec 4.12)

CO: reduces oxygen carried by blood
teach.note: Sources: burning fuels with sulfur; incomplete combustion.

teach.heading: Greenhouse effect (spec 4.13 to 4.15)
bullets: Human activity: burning fuels (CO₂), cattle and rice (methane), fertilisers (N₂O)
Consequences: rising sea level, extreme weather, habitat change
teach.note: Enhanced, not the natural effect, is the problem.

teach.heading: Water pollution (spec 4.16, 4.17)
bullets: Decomposers use up oxygen; fish die
teach.note: Eutrophication sequence: learn in order.

teach.heading: Timed section rules
teach.note: One mark a minute.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Why do fish die in eutrophication?
options: Bacteria use up the oxygen decomposing dead plants
